summary: LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates. We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.
title: Contexture: Runtime Context Eviction for High-Throughput Agent Serving

summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) has become a core technique for post-training large language models, enabling students to learn from dense token-level supervision on their own generations. However, even with a capable teacher, OPD training can be unstable, leading to excessive response length, repetitive generation, and severe performance degradation. One example is \textit{spurious agreement}, where the student maintains high overlap with the teacher at the states visited but produces repetitive generations. Although such failures have been observed, the mechanisms behind these failures remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we investigate OPD through the lens of learning dynamics, tracing three mechanisms from local analysis to subsequent on-policy sampling. We first identify states where sampled-token OPD updates fail to correct teacher--student mismatch and characterize them using the student's mass on the teacher's top-$p$ set. We then show that learning from the teacher is difficult at mismatched states and that their gradients can also affect with learning at other tokens. Finally, using a termination-token mismatch as a case study, we study how continued training on mismatched states influences on-policy sampling, suppressing the student's current modes and leading the student toward states where the teacher is unreliable . These findings help explain the benefits of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization and motivate targeted correction of states where student and teacher are mismatched.

summary: Vision-language models for medical image segmentation often produce masks that conflict with the accompanying text, especially under multi-site/multi-lesion descriptions. We trace this failure to two factors: (i) highly templated and repetitive clinical language causes one-to-one hard contrastive learning to yield numerous false negatives, weakening cross-modal alignment; and (ii) predominantly vision-driven, one-way cross-attention lacks a language-dominant, spatially aware pathway, hindering effective injection of textual semantics into the spatial visual domain. To this end, we propose Consistency-enhanced Two-stage Segmentation (C2Seg). In the pretraining stage, Cluster-aware Contrastive Learning uses a frozen strong baseline to construct an intra-batch text similarity matrix as soft labels, thereby alleviating false negative conflicts and producing more discriminative visual representations. In the fusion stage, we introduce a Bidirectional Complementary Attention Module, where each modality dominates attention along its own path, fostering deep interaction and structural consistency between visual and textual representations. In order to enhance the expressive power of multimodal features, we further adopt KAN-based Attention Gating. Without updating the language encoder, our approach significantly improves text-mask consistency and segmentation accuracy on four public medical imaging datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/JGuiidev/C2Seg.
title: Towards Text-Mask Consistency in Medical Image Segmentation

summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong video comprehension, largely benefiting from extensive training on realistic video data. However, when video perception severely conflicts with internal priors or common sense, we identify a critical failure pattern termed Modal Polarization, where models fail to integrate modalities and instead bifurcate into two distinct extremes: Cognitive Inertia, where models rigidly adhere to priors despite contradictory visual evidence, and Perceptual Inertia, where they blindly trust video perception while ignoring logical inconsistencies. To investigate this, we introduce TheaterBench, a benchmark designed to expose Modal Polarization using counter-intuitive scenarios that violate physical laws or common sense - situations rarely encountered in standard training distributions. Extensive experiments reveal that current state-of-the-art (SOTA) models exhibit severe Modal Polarization, and many de-hallucination methods merely rebalance the trade-off between Perceptual and Cognitive Inertia rather than fundamentally resolving the conflict. This work serves as a foundational step for evaluating and enhancing the perceptual-cognitive equilibrium of future video understanding models.

summary: Agentic products introduce risks that extend beyond those of their underlying models, arising from their tools, permissions, data access, safeguards, and operating conditions. Existing evaluation instruments provide useful evidence about model behavior and agents in defined harnesses, but their results do not necessarily transfer to deployed products or cover risks created by product configurations and interactions. Identifying and measuring such risks is especially difficult before deployment, when failure pathways, exposure, and outcome distributions may be poorly understood. This raises a fundamental question: what can evaluation evidence establish about the safety of a particular product, and what decisions can it legitimately support? We call the illusion of evaluation the appearance of safety assurance when producing an evaluation result is treated as sufficient evidence for claims that extend beyond what was measured. Drawing on practitioner experience, prior research, and twelve illustrative product contexts, we identify six methodological challenges spanning product-risk identification, ecological and measurement validity, metric interpretation, outcome verification, evidence transfer, and evidentiary sufficiency. We propose a granular transparency-and-decision-relevance record that makes risks, system configurations, assumptions, uncertainty, and evidentiary limits explicit. The proposal is a reporting and reasoning aid, not proof of safety or a deployment-approval standard. We conclude with open questions on valid product-level measurements, evidence transfer, and decision sufficiency.

summary: Improving agents requires discovering where they fail and understanding why. An agent acts over multiple steps in a changing environment, so diagnosing its failures requires more than inspecting the final response of a large language model (LLM). The same unsuccessful outcome can arise from task difficulty or from an error the agent repeats across tasks. We introduce ProbeAgent, an automated framework that discovers agent failures, tests their proposed causes, and identifies shared failure modes. Starting from benchmark tasks, ProbeAgent builds executable tests and validates them using reference solutions, automated checks, and review of the task requirements. For each failed trajectory, it explains the error and constructs new tasks that preserve the suspected cause while changing the surrounding context. Running the agent on these tasks tests whether the same error recurs. ProbeAgent then groups failures with similar causes and generates descriptions that distinguish their errors. This process connects explanations of individual failures to executable tests and descriptions of shared failure modes. We evaluate ProbeAgent across 22 agent configurations using tasks from 10 benchmarks, collecting 1,244 failures and producing 536 failure-mode descriptions. These descriptions distinguish specific errors within broad outcomes such as incomplete work, including planning without acting and stopping before delivering a file. In human evaluation, annotators accept 90.0% of assigned descriptions and correctly reject 83.3% of similar alternatives, supporting the accuracy and specificity of the discovered failure modes.
title: ProbeAgent: Principled Diagnosis of Agent Failures in Verifiable Environments

summary: Traffic forecasting models are typically evaluated under ideal conditions with complete data. This evaluation does not reflect the frequent sensor failures and communication outages common in real-world deployments. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of multivariate traffic prediction models to evaluate their performance under varying levels of sensor data loss during inference. We benchmark several architectural paradigms, including graph neural networks, attention-based Transformers, and selective state-space models, across sparsity levels ranging from zero to complete sensor loss, using two widely used multi-channel traffic benchmarks. To ensure consistent comparison across traffic variables, we use normalized metrics and define a usability threshold to identify when predictions become unreliable. Our results show a clear trade-off between baseline accuracy and robustness: models with the highest accuracy under full-data conditions often degrade most sharply as data becomes sparse, while less accurate models maintain more stable performance. These findings show that model selection should be based on the expected reliability of the sensor network rather than peak accuracy alone. This work provides a practical framework for assessing traffic forecasting models and highlights the importance of robustness in real-world applications.

summary: Trading agents join probabilistic language-model inference to persistent portfolio state and execution authority. A false claim can become an order, an evaluator flaw can promote a worse policy, and shared models or data can produce correlated behavior. AI-safety research studies reward misspecification, tool misuse, distribution shift, evaluation gaming, and unsafe self-modification. Financial research and governance study execution costs, market access, manipulation, operational resilience, backtest overfitting, and systemic feedback. These literatures are rarely integrated into one measurement agenda for systems that reason in language and act in markets. This paper defines the relevant system boundary and develops four conjectures with twelve measurable research subproblems: grounding and abstention; user-mandate fidelity; bounded information and execution authority; leakage-resistant evaluation; execution fidelity; promotion-gate integrity; emergent manipulation; correlated stress; tacit coordination; provenance and position-policy continuity; deterministic risk kernels and interruption; and human governance and recovery. Each subproblem specifies a failure pathway, research question, minimum experiment, metrics, and deployment implication. The supporting evidence map (Appendix A) distinguishes direct trading-agent evidence, market-mechanism evidence, general AI-safety evidence, official governance precedents, and author proposals. The paper also proposes a ten-part reporting standard and a set of anti-problems: higher returns, benchmark scores, more explanation, more autonomy, more agents, or a passed model judge do not by themselves constitute safety progress. This is a structured research agenda, not a systematic review, empirical validation, or claim that any architecture makes autonomous trading safe.

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Light through a Jerlov water type. summary: Abstract Reliable rare-flood decisions require more than numerical convergence or pooled interval coverage. We evaluate a reporting framework that distinguishes reporting (PASS), seeking further information (HOLD), and withholding an unsupported estimate for review (WITHHOLD). Five policies were compared on shared simulated cases in a post-development frozen V11 evaluation cohort (2,800 cases) and a separately targeted stress cohort (2,000 cases), using selective coverage, acceptance, paired illustrative loss, and cost sensitivity. V11 accepted 657/2,800 (23.46%) cases in the frozen cohort; 637/657 accepted intervals covered the true target (96.96%). In targeted stress, it accepted 23/2,000 (1.15%), of which 9/23 (39.13%) covered truth; all five heavy-tail GEV cells had zero PASS. V11's mean proxy loss exceeded that of the V10 decision candidate in the frozen cohort (0.8118 versus 0.7585) but was lower in targeted stress (1.5017 versus 1.7258); policy rankings also varied across 180 assumed cost settings. An earlier external Powell audit reported 11/2,000 heavy-tail discrepancies, but did not establish case identity or objective equivalence. Replaying the eleven named cases from the archived V11 generator recovered the reference point estimates; independent profile-interval validation remains unresolved. Five Australian gauge series comprise annual maxima of daily-mean flow, not instantaneous peaks; penalized GEV did not outperform lognormal on mean expanding-origin log score at four comparable gauges. The results map simulation-specific failure domains and decision trade-offs; they do not validate a general screening guarantee or a facility design recommendation. Keywords: flood-frequency analysis; generalized extreme value; selective coverage; abstention; decision loss; heavy tails; temporal dependence; out-of-sample validation.

We evaluate a reporting framework that distinguishes reporting (PASS), seeking further information (HOLD), and withholding an unsupported estimate for review (WITHHOLD). Five policies were compared on shared simulated cases in a post-development frozen V11 evaluation cohort (2,800 cases) and a separately targeted stress cohort (2,000 cases), using selective coverage, acceptance, paired illustrative loss, and cost sensitivity. V11 accepted 657/2,800 (23.46%) cases in the frozen cohort; 637/657 accepted intervals covered the true target (96.96%). In targeted stress, it accepted 23/2,000 (1.15%), of which 9/23 (39.13%) covered truth; all five heavy-tail GEV cells had zero PASS. V11's mean proxy loss exceeded that of the V10 decision candidate in the frozen cohort (0.8118 versus 0.7585) but was lower in targeted stress (1.5017 versus 1.7258); policy rankings also varied across 180 assumed cost settings. An earlier external Powell audit reported 11/2,000 heavy-tail discrepancies, but did not establish case identity or objective equivalence. Replaying the eleven named cases from the archived V11 generator recovered the reference point estimates; independent profile-interval validation remains unresolved. Five Australian gauge series comprise annual maxima of daily-mean flow, not instantaneous peaks; penalized GEV did not outperform lognormal on mean expanding-origin log score at four comparable gauges. The results map simulation-specific failure domains and decision trade-offs; they do not validate a general screening guarantee or a facility design recommendation. Keywords: flood-frequency analysis; generalized extreme value; selective coverage; abstention; decision loss; heavy tails; temporal dependence; out-of-sample validation.

summary: The growing complexity of electronic systems demands efficient design flows, yet EDA scripting remains a bottleneck: proprietary APIs are sparsely documented, and errors often appear as silent failures or cryptic exceptions. Hand-crafted knowledge helps but is difficult to maintain as toolchains evolve. We present ZhuLong-SE (Self-Evolution), an execution-grounded LLM agent that learns reusable knowledge from prior task traces. Building on ZhuLong, it enhances the task-level harness with API retrieval, documentation responses, isolated sandbox execution, and static checking, then adds governed cross-task self-evolution. Beyond solving individual tasks, ZhuLong-SE distills past execution traces into a three-tier memory store governed by ground-truth anchoring, disconfirmation filtering, held-out rollback, and anti-leakage retrieval. On the 158-task EDA-Eval-PyAether benchmark, the full task-level harness, with self-evolution disabled, achieves 92.4% pass@1 and outperforms ZhuLong on all five tested LLM backbones. On a harder instance-disjoint test set, self-evolution from the bare configuration surpasses a human-crafted-experience baseline by 2.5 percentage points (80.0% vs. 77.5% pass@1).
title: Self-Evolving Beyond Human-Crafted Experience for EDA Scripting

summary: Generative models now write working code, produce realistic images, and hold long conversations, yet the mechanisms behind their intelligence still evade our understanding. This thesis explores that puzzle through Associative Memory (AM), in which patterns are stored as energy minima and retrieved through attractor dynamics. Beyond their capacity, AMs form new minima known as spurious states, long regarded as a failure of memory. We argue that this failure is where creativity begins, and that memorization and generalization can coexist as outcomes of one retrieval process. First, we show that diffusion models behave as AMs. With little data, a diffusion model forms a distinct basin of attraction around each training sample. As the data grows, these basins shrink, and spurious states emerge as attractors that blend stored samples yet match none of them. They are the first signs of generative capability. We characterize this transition by measuring the volume, energy, and curvature of these basins across datasets and architectures, including Stable Diffusion. We then turn to language and move beyond the energy-based view of AM. We show that uniform-state discrete diffusion models are AMs capable of retrieving unseen data, with basins of attraction that arise from conditional likelihood maximization alone. As the training set grows, basins around training examples contract while basins around unseen examples expand, until corrupted test sentences are recovered as reliably as training ones. Conditional entropy exposes this coexistence within a single sequence and cheaply diagnoses where a model lies along the transition. Together, these results suggest that AM is a general principle defined by basins of attraction, and that memorization and generalization can coexist within one model. AM thus offers a framework for asking when a generative model recalls and when it creates.
title: Memorization and Generalization in Generative Models: A Perspective From Energy-based Modeling and Associative Memory

summary: The MoT virtual environment, called the Metaverse of Things (MoT), combines machine learning (ML) and Internet of Things (IoT) to offer significant business opportunities in various sectors such as entertainment, healthcare, and education. In addition to its benefits, the MoT poses risks to privacy and security through unauthorized access, which threatens trustworthiness. While traditional intrusion detection systems (IDS) exist to handle this challenge, they struggle with high-dimensional data and poor interpretability. To address this challenge, the research conducted a thorough analysis of different ML models and proposed the optimal model to secure the MoT environment. The research employed explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to identify the most effective features that contributed to optimal model selection. The research presented an optimal framework combining ML and XAI to safeguard MoT networks from the most recent cyberthreats. The research used three advanced benchmark security datasets: ToN-IoT, CIC-IoT-2023, and BoT-IoT, to examine the XAI-based intrusion detection framework. The XAI-based intrusion detection framework achieved 99.83% accuracy on ToN-IoT and 96.45% on CIC-IoT-2023 using the XGBoost model. On the BoT-IoT dataset, the Random Forest (RF) and Extra Trees (ET) classifiers reached 99.99% accuracy. The Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) techniques used for XAI further enhanced feature relevance and user confidence in the optimal model.
title: Enhancing Metaverse Security using Explainable AI-based Intrusion Detection Framework

summary: Vision-model-based robotic navigation has gained increasing popularity, yet existing approaches still struggle to deliver effective and efficient navigation performance, \textit{e.g.}, diffusion-based policies that require costly iterative denoising. In this work, we propose three improvements to bridge these gaps. First, we adopt a rectified flow framework to reduce the required inference steps to one while achieving comparable or even superior performance. Second, we leverage a bidirectional Mamba-based visual encoder that employs selective state-space modeling to more effectively capture bidirectional temporal dependencies across observation frames, even with longer input sequences. Most importantly, we find that naïvely combining these two components to balance accuracy with inference speed yields no further performance gains or even produces inferior results. Upon extensive analysis, we realized that the root cause lies in the fact that the Hydra-derived temporal context is shared unchanged across all flow timesteps, and timestep information is introduced only within the velocity network. This weak coupling limits the model's ability to adaptively exploit temporal visual features at different flow states. To address this, we propose a feature-wise timestep conditioning design that explicitly conditions the visual embedding on the flow timestep, enabling noise-level-aware trajectory generation, thereby restoring a meaningful gradient pathway and enabling coherent interaction between the rectified flow and the temporal encoder. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms both baseline and competitive methods.
title: Inject, Encode, Navigate: Feature-Wise Time Injection for Rectified Flow with Bidirectional Feature Encoding

summary: Vector databases support semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation, but embeddings, queries, and record labels may contain sensitive information. Although encrypted vector search protects these contents, some schemes expose records retrieved together across queries. We identify semantic neighborhood leakage, whereby co-retrieval relationships derived from access patterns reveal semantic categories of encrypted records and queries. We present SAGE (Semantic Access-pattern Graph Exploitation), a passive, persistent leakage-abuse attack that infers record labels and query categories from access patterns. SAGE builds a weighted co-retrieval graph and offers two variants requiring different auxiliary knowledge. SAGE-Dist matches anonymous spectral groups to semantic categories using estimated class proportions and refines labels via optimal transport, without known record labels. SAGE-Known combines graph-based label propagation with spectral-group anchor voting using a small set of known labels. We evaluate SAGE on four text and image datasets. With 1% known record labels, SAGE-Known achieves up to 84.3% mean record-label accuracy and outperforms the strongest corresponding baselines on all four datasets. With only estimated class proportions, SAGE-Dist achieves 66.9% record-label accuracy and 68.1% query-category accuracy on AG News, exceeding the strongest corresponding baselines by 21.8 and 41.9 percentage points, respectively, though performance varies across datasets. Experiments with a real-world DCPE implementation (Fuchsbauer et al., SCN'22) show that semantic leakage persists under encrypted approximate retrieval. These findings expose privacy risks even when vector contents remain protected.
title: "More Than You Expect!": Leakage-Abuse Attacks on Encrypted Vector Search

summary: LLM-generated descriptions enrich zero-shot skeleton-based action recognition but repeat cues shared by confusable actions. Their contextual semantics also lack explicit links to skeleton features. To address these challenges, we propose CRAFT, which couples Concept Refinement and Feature-grounded Tokens. Hard-negative-conditioned generation and contrastive scoring identify concepts that distinguish each action from its closest rivals. Unique-QDPP selects complementary descriptions within each semantic slot and prevents their reuse across slots. This bank supervises learnable concept tokens that read motion and context cues from each skeleton. On fixed NTU-60 and NTU-120 splits, CRAFT improves five baselines spanning four recognition paradigms. ZSL accuracy and GZSL harmonic mean increase on every baseline-split pair, by 5.4 and 5.9 percentage points on average. Random-split experiments extend these gains to three datasets, including PKU-MMD. Code will be released after acceptance.
title: Crafting the Difference, Grounding the Evidence: Discriminative Concept Learning for Zero-Shot Skeleton Action Recognition

summary: Assigning tenants to separate GPUs does not isolate their host memory traffic. We identify an unprivileged timing channel between GPUs without NVLink: a co-tenant can detect contention by timing reads to its own pinned host buffer, without accessing victim data or using hardware performance counters. The signal tracks the number of distinct host pages the victim touches rather than its throughput. We demonstrate covert communication at 20 bit/s with near-zero error, LLM output-length inference at a held-out Spearman correlation of 0.99 across five models on three platforms, and refusal inference at balanced accuracy up to 0.955. The attacks cross process, container, and Unix-user boundaries and reproduce across two GPU generations and two serving runtimes. Bursty transfers in the tested vLLM+LMCache stack remain below the leakage floor, limiting the demonstrated attacks to sustained device-to-host traffic. IOMMU-disabled and cross-NUMA controls attribute the channel to page-walk contention at the shared host memory controller. This finding motivates two defenses, controller-aware placement and footprint flattening, both of which reduce inference to chance in our experiments. Accelerator isolation alone does not isolate the host infrastructure that tenants share.
title: A Footprint-Sensitive Cross-GPU Timing Channel Through the Shared Host Memory Subsystem

summary: Offshore wind planning requires balancing capital cost, wind-resource potential, and seabird exposure. We formulate a spatial tri-objective mixed-integer linear program for offshore wind capacity allocation, minimizing capital cost and modeled seabird exposure while maximizing wind-weighted capacity. Applied to Australia's Gippsland offshore wind area, the model identifies exposure reductions of 23-44% at capital-cost premiums of 0.8-6.1% across 15 wind-weighted capacity requirements. We benchmark exposure-aware optimization against 19 percentile-based exclusion thresholds. At a fixed wind-weighted capacity requirement, the 5th-percentile threshold reduces exposure by 30.1% at a 37.6% cost premium, versus at least 30.1% at a 1.4% premium with optimization. Under a fixed capital budget, exclusion screening reduces exposure by 48.2% with a 26.9% capacity loss, compared with 48.5% and 7.6%, respectively, under optimization. These results highlight the value of explicitly optimizing graded seabird exposure.
title: Seabird-Aware Multi-Objective Offshore Wind Capacity Allocation: A Gippsland Case Study

summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) represent each image with hundreds of visual tokens, which can make inference costly even when a prompt depends on only part of the image. Dynamic Token Merging (DTM), introduced in MrT5 for byte-level text encoders, learns which tokens to remove: a lightweight delete gate scores contextualized hidden states, acts as a differentiable attention bias during training, and physically removes tokens at inference. We argue that DTM is a general token deletion framework rather than a byte-level technique, and extend it to the vision modality and to decoder-only models. Applying DTM to T5Gemma 2 and Gemma 3 yields V-MrT5Gemma2, which deletes visual tokens inside a bidirectional multimodal encoder, and V-MrGemma3, which compacts the prompt and its key-value caches during decoder-only prefill. Across ten benchmarks, DTM's advantage over attention-based and random deletion grows with the deletion rate and is largest on document, chart, and scene-text reading. At 80% visual token deletion (approximately 60% fewer FLOPs), DTM raises accuracy over FastV from 51.8 to 63.0 on ChartQA and from 63.3 to 67.8 on TextVQA with V-MrT5Gemma2, as well as from 62.2 to 68.8 and from 71.2 to 75.1 with V-MrGemma3, retaining 90-96% of unpruned performance on both tasks with significant efficiency gains. These results support DTM as a general framework for efficient transformers.

summary: In this paper we introduce a new benchmark dataset, NightmareDiscourseBench, for testing NLP pipelines that identify forms of direct discourse in English-language fiction. We first review existing publicly available benchmarks (providing summary statistics and reviewing available metadata) for this task, identifying theoretical inconsistency and exclusive focus on speech as primary issues in this domain. We then overview our narrative theory-based framework for classifying and evaluating different forms of direct discourse, and finally describe NightmareDiscourseBench, a new benchmark test set of 12 text samples accompanied by metadata pertinent to the task of direct discourse identification.

summary: Conventional indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks hijack an LLM agent's workflow through malicious instructions embedded in retrieved external content. The growing adoption of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) exposes another attack surface: tool descriptions supplied by third-party MCP servers. Attackers can manipulate this metadata to induce malicious argument generation during tool calls. The challenge is to ensure that the modified descriptions still appear benign to both LLMs and users. Existing IPI attacks, however, struggle to achieve both high attack success and low detectability in this setting. To address this challenge, we propose GRAFT, an LLM-based optimization method for crafting adversarial tool descriptions. Specifically, GRAFT uses a masking mechanism to identify argument-relevant token positions for targeted injection. It then iteratively refines candidate descriptions using dynamic mutation strategies proposed by an LLM, guided by the agent's tool choices and generated arguments. We evaluate GRAFT on three public datasets against several attack baselines. The results show that GRAFT achieves higher attack success while maintaining low detection rates across five filter-based defenses. It also bypasses several existing IPI defenses. Even under an adaptive defense trained on GRAFT-generated injections, GRAFT remains more effective than the baselines.
title: Subverting Tool Arguments: Defense-Evading Metadata Poisoning in LLM Agents

summary: Hybrid density functional theory calculations were used to investigate the stability, electronic properties, and catalytic activity of transition-metal impurities substituting Zn sites (M\(_{\rm Zn}\)) in the MOF-5 metal-organic framework [Zn\(_4\)O(BDC)\(_3\), BDC = 1,4-benzenedicarboxylate], with M = Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, and Cu. Most substitutions introduce \(3d\) states within the MOF-5 band gap and induce localized magnetic moments. Partially occupied \(3d\) states promote orbital hybridization and charge transfer with oxygenated intermediates, activating the dopant sites toward oxygen electrocatalysis. The oxygen reduction and evolution reaction (ORR and OER) activities were evaluated using the computational hydrogen electrode model. Mn\(_{\rm Zn}\) and Fe\(_{\rm Zn}\) exhibit calculated ORR overpotentials of 0.57~V, while Mn\(_{\rm Zn}\) and Co\(_{\rm Zn}\) yield OER overpotentials of 0.42 and 0.51~V, respectively, approaching those of benchmark precious-metal electrocatalysts. These findings identify Mn substitution as a promising strategy for achieving bifunctional ORR/OER activity in MOF-5 and establish a link between dopant electronic structure and catalytic performance to guide the design of MOF-based electrocatalysts.
title: Transition-Metal Substitutions in MOF-5: A Hybrid-DFT Study of Oxygen Electrocatalysis

summary: Hybrid density functional theory calculations were used to investigate the stability, electronic properties, and catalytic activity of transition-metal impurities substituting Zn sites (M\(_{\rm Zn}\)) in the MOF-5 metal-organic framework [Zn\(_4\)O(BDC)\(_3\), BDC = 1,4-benzenedicarboxylate], with M = Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, and Cu. Most substitutions introduce \(3d\) states within the MOF-5 band gap and induce localized magnetic moments. Partially occupied \(3d\) states promote orbital hybridization and charge transfer with oxygenated intermediates, activating the dopant sites toward oxygen electrocatalysis. The oxygen reduction and evolution reaction (ORR and OER) activities were evaluated using the computational hydrogen electrode model. Mn\(_{\rm Zn}\) and Fe\(_{\rm Zn}\) exhibit calculated ORR overpotentials of 0.57~V, while Mn\(_{\rm Zn}\) and Co\(_{\rm Zn}\) yield OER overpotentials of 0.42 and 0.51~V, respectively, approaching those of benchmark precious-metal electrocatalysts. These findings identify Mn substitution as a promising strategy for achieving bifunctional ORR/OER activity in MOF-5 and establish a link between dopant electronic structure and catalytic performance to guide the design of MOF-based electrocatalysts.

summary: DeepCatch v2.3.0 is an open-source cfDNA fragmentomics benchmark that is validated on public data the model has never been trained on. A 5-channel DELFI profile (5 Mb / 100 kb ratios and coverage, plus a 196-bin fragment-size distribution) is extracted from publicly served FinaleDB fragment files and scored with a per-study harmonised PCA + logistic-regression pipeline. Training on FinaleDB publications 6 + 8 (n=627) and testing on held-out publications 1, 7 and 9 gives an external AUC of 0.9444 [0.8731, 1.0000] on one whole-genome publication (n=31), 0.708 [0.5148, 0.9012] on a second (n=52), and 0.7385 [0.6281, 0.8488] pooled over the publications carrying both classes; the whole-exome publication transfers only partly (breast 0.6938, prostate 0.7127). Transfer between whole-genome studies is real but far from uniform, and the assay platform blunts it further. A leave-one-study-out run inside the training cohort gives 0.6805, so the pooled 0.9684 is reported as a within-cohort separation number rather than a generalisation claim. The multi-modal stage is carried by a regularized late fusion (AUC 0.9825) and a Bayesian model average (0.9650) rather than the neural encoder (0.554) at this sample size. The methylation path runs end to end on real public fragment data. Not clinically validated; research use only.

summary: This dataset supports the manuscript “Which physiological parameters remain recoverable after quantum encoding? A few-qubit study of voice, ECG, PPG and EEG.” The study evaluates recovery of 33 known physiological parameters from simulated biosignals after five quantum encoding schemes. Recovery is assessed using classical probes fitted to selected quantum observables and compared with raw descriptors and classical controls. Separate analyses evaluate prediction performance on clinical datasets. The record contains three archives. • synthetic-data.zip contains synthetic voice, ECG, PPG and EEG datasets, including generated records, ground-truth parameters and available extracted descriptors. It includes development, test, separately generated test and seed-sensitivity datasets. • analysis-results.zip contains saved benchmark and follow-up outputs, including result tables, paired contrasts, run manifests and predictions where available. Follow-up analyses include benchmark voice qubit reallocation and fixed-input angle-PCA controls that vary CZ gates and readout observables. • clinical-figure-support.zip contains aggregate clinical scores and paired intervals used to generate the clinical prediction figure, together with plotted-value tables for the reviewer-control figures. It does not contain individual clinical recordings or participant-level predictions.   The study protocol and multimodal update are recorded at https://osf.io/m7tkg/ . This supporting-data deposit does not establish or alter the timing of preregistration.

summary: Visual geo-localization of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in GNSS-denied environments is hindered by a lack of datasets combining sequential acquisition, broad geographic coverage, multi-modal imagery, and diverse flying heights. To address this, we present UAV-VisLoc, a dataset of 14,998 sequential UAV images in 30 flights paired with over 118,000 georeferenced satellite tiles for visual geo-localization. The images cover seven scene types and include both RGB and infrared images. The dataset consists of two subsets. The real-flight subset (flights 01–21, 11,476 images) was captured onboard along flight paths in China at flying heights of about 120–850 m above the ground. The orthoimage-derived subset (flights 22–30, 3,522 images) was cropped along predefined paths from OpenAerialMap orthoimages covering areas on six continents. Image-level metadata and ground-truth annotations are provided. A data quality validation confirms metadata consistency, positioning accuracy, annotation reliability, and image quality. In addition, baseline experiments on the real-flight subset demonstrate the utility of the dataset.

summary: Numerical data and MATLAB source code accompanying the study "Input-aware neural residual learning and disturbance estimation in constrained model predictive control for vessel dynamic positioning" by Nguyen Quang Duy and Nguyen Van Suong. summary: Local LLM assistants decode for one user at a time, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and leaves compute idle. Streaming safety checks today trade accuracy against cost. A dedicated guard model is accurate but nearly doubles the latency per token, while a hidden-state probe is cheap but less accurate. We present ToRA, an adapter that runs a second model as an extra row in the generator's decode step, sharing its weights and KV cache. Dual-row kernels read each weight once for both rows. On Qwen3-0.6B, ToRA matches or beats a dedicated streaming guard, with higher F1 on 12 of 17 benchmarks. It detects 11.8 points more unsafe responses than the probe at a similar cost, under 4% added latency per token.
title: Run One, Get Two: Near-Free Streaming Safety Checks for Local LLMs

summary: LLM agents are expected to improve themselves from their own experience across episodes, with fixed weights. Self-improvement in an embodied world cannot be read from one measure. Existing benchmarks measure task progress, world-knowledge question answering (QA), and episodic memory, but a correct answer does not show that the agent ever observed the evidence for it, and progress does not show what the agent learned. We introduce AstronautBench, which measures one agent's self-improvement through three views on the same run: what it knows, whether its own evidence supports that knowledge, and how far it gets in the world. It is built on the game Outer Wilds, where each episode is a 22-minute loop after which the world resets, only the agent's knowledge carries over, and progress is gated by knowledge. After every episode, we measure the places reached and ship-log rumor facts revealed, the correctness of answers to 164 questions about the world, and whether each answer is supported by the frames and position the agent cites from its own recorded play. Two LLM judges from different model families check every answer. In eight-episode baselines with GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon planners, which act through a learned controller or their own gamepad inputs, the three views do not move together, so any one of them alone gives an incomplete picture of whether the agent is improving. The GPT-6.1 Sol agent's correct answers grow from 14.6% to 26.8% of all questions, but at episode 8 only 59 to 68% of them are supported by its cited evidence. It reveals no new rumor facts after episode 3, while the places it reaches and its memory keep growing. More than half of the answers that become correct after episode 3 cite only evidence from earlier episodes.
title: AstronautBench: Measuring Agent Self-Improvement Across Episodes Through Knowledge, Evidence, and Progress

summary: Strain localization is often associated with plastic flow and permanent deformation. Here we show that a tensile neck in a crosslinked nematic network can undergo nearly complete recovery through reverse phase-boundary motion, leaving little residual deformation. In a monodomain liquid crystal elastomer stretched perpendicular to its initial director, this recovery occurs during an isothermal loading-unloading cycle. Digital image correlation resolves the process as the retreat of interfaces separating low- and high-stretch regions, where the high-stretch domain shrinks while previously necked material thickens, despite substantial mechanical hysteresis. Within the recoverable-necking regime, increasing temperature lowers the loading plateau stress but raises the unloading plateau stress. A nonconvex constitutive description provides an energetic basis for the coexistence of the two stretch states, while gradient regularization accounts for the finite width of their interfaces through an equilibrium reference profile. These results identify the spatial mechanism of neck recovery and distinguish recoverable strain localization from mechanical reversibility in an orientationally ordered polymer network.

summary: Grain boundaries (GBs) govern many properties of polycrystalline materials, and inverse design would make the GB structure itself a design variable. Crystal generative models such as MatterGen operate on periodic cells, which contain two GBs. The cell energy defines a single GB only when the two are equivalent, but existing models do not enforce this equivalence. Building on MatterGen, we developed a symmetry-constrained diffusion model in which the two GBs are related by a symmetry operation: atoms near one GB are generated, and those near the other are reconstructed through a symmetry projection applied at every denoising step. We applied it to the $Σ5(210)[001]$ symmetric tilt GB in Al, conditioning generation on the GB energy from a machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP). All 350 generated structures kept a geometrically equivalent GB pair after relaxation. Given a target GB energy, the model generated structures at that energy: for the three in-range targets with many nearby training structures, 44% to 70% fell within $\pm 0.1$ J/m$^2$ of the target. Tracking weakened at higher energies and failed outside the training range. Of the 91 near-target structures, 90 matched no training structure under the adopted geometric criterion, indicating that the model can propose configurations near the target energy that are distinct from the training structures, a capability that could help identify unknown metastable GB structures observed in experiments. Building GB-pair equivalence into generation thus makes GB properties well-defined design targets, enabling inverse design of GB structures.
title: Generating grain boundary structures at a specified energy with a symmetry-constrained diffusion model

summary: Time-Fractional derivatives (TFDs) have been widely used in mathematical modeling of physical phenomena such as anomalous diffusion and memory effects of materials. Traditionally, TFD is handled {either by a direct method which saves almost all the memory and hence computationally expensive or a sum of exponential method (SOE) which decomposes the time domain improper integral into a local term and a history term} {approximated by} a sum of exponential functions. The limitation of the SOE approach is that{ the approximation error of the local term might result in large errors if the unknown function is not smooth enough at $0$ and can lead to over-dissipation of energy.} In this paper, we take a different approach and will focus on the Caputo derivative because the Caputo time derivative of a constant function is 0. We present a simple time-stepping algorithm based on the theory of Stieltjes-Markov functions, a subclass of the Herglotz-Nevanlinna functions. The key is in identifying the Stieltjes-Markov function structure hidden in the Laplace transform of the kernel function. Compared to most of the current methods in literature, the novelty of the results in this paper is manifold. First, no decomposition of integral is needed and our resulting approximation in the time domain contains a Dirac measure with carefully calculated strength, leading to a drastic decrease in the number of exponential functions needed in the approximation. Secondly, the choice of our interpolation points is based on the Mellin's inversion theorem and hence the interpolation error in the transformed domain is explicitly and rigorously linked to the error in the time-domain. {Finally, the resulting system is almost diagonal and hence can be easily sped up by using the Schur complement method.}
title: A Higher-Order Algorithm for Solving Time-Fractional Differential Equations via Rational Approximation of z^α as a Herglotz-Nevanlinna function

summary: We investigate the information retained by fuzzy-point specialization in Chang fuzzy topologies and the fibers realizing a prescribed Gödel specialization relation. Every reflexive, minimum-transitive fuzzy preorder has a greatest stratified Chang realization. Its realization fiber is a singleton precisely for the constant relation $1$; otherwise, below each member lies a continuum-sized descending chain with no lower bound in the fiber, also within the Alexandrov subclass. On finite support sets, every nontrivial stratified fiber has cardinality continuum without assuming Alexandrov completeness; this remains true for Alexandrov fibers on countable sets. We describe the entire two-point Alexandrov fiber order as the reverse of a product of classes of join-preserving threshold functions. For arbitrary Chang topologies, quasi-specialization determines membership specialization and its kernel completion, which in turn determine Gödel specialization; the converse determinations fail in general. A central reconstruction result identifies the greatest quasi-specialization realization by \emph{exact agreement on every one- or two-point restriction}, equivalently by closure in a product of discrete grade intervals. In particular, quasi-specialization determines every Chang topology on a finite support set. We also represent general Alexandrov Chang topologies by matrices of join-preserving threshold maps and isolate the additional scalar compatibility law required for reconstruction from the graded relation. These results separate information encoded by finite-coordinate point comparisons from global restrictions on fuzzy open families.

summary: Particle picking is a key step in single-particle cryo-electron microscopy. It is a challenging task where tomographic projections of proteins and other macromolecules are identified in extremely noisy images. In this work, we introduce a particle picker based on a seminorm defined in terms of a fast wavelet approximation to the earth mover's distance. Our picker is template-free, self-supervised and does not require any prior knowledge of the molecules of interest other than their approximate size. We test it on three public datasets and show that it achieves state-of-the-art reconstructions.
title: Particle picking with an earth mover's seminorm

summary: We demonstrate that weight-space programming and edits guided by sparse autoencoders can remove unwanted aspects of a particle-physics foundation model through direct edits to its weights. In a foundation model trained on jets, we observe that adding a single soft neutral particle causes large changes in jet classification, violating infrared safety. We locate the responsible attention heads with mechanistic analysis and trace the flaw's origin to pretraining on datasets with different reconstruction thresholds. We then propose two targeted approaches to repair the flaw: by removing three latent directions identified with sparse autoencoders, and by letting language-model agents edit the weights directly, without gradients and with only 50 queries to the model. Both their edits individually remove almost the entire flaw and leave the rest of the model's response nearly unchanged. Compared to fine-tuning, both methods change far fewer parameters. Although built only on $W$ and QCD jets, the edits carry over to all signal classes, the pretrained generator, and a newly trained regression head.
title: Weight-space programming and mechanistic interpretability for model editing in particle physics

summary: We examined the association between submission of an assessment by day 30 and final course outcome in the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD). To avoid classifying students who withdrew during the exposure window as comparable non-submitters, the main analysis was restricted to students enrolled at a day-30 landmark. In the CCC/2014J course presentation, 1,820 students remained after exclusions for missing covariates and unsupported exposure categories; 1,624 had submitted at least one non-banked assessment by day 30. The difference in favorable final outcome rates (Pass or Distinction) was 0.3743. A normalized inverse-probability-weighted contrast was 0.3861 (95% full-refit bootstrap interval 0.3242 to 0.4447). The overlap-weighted contrast was 0.3261 (0.2667 to 0.3870), describing a different weighted population. The weights were unstable in the smaller comparison group, and measured covariates remained imbalanced under inverse-probability weighting. We independently reconstructed the cohort and estimates from the official UCI archive, examined eligibility and missing-data exclusions, and repeated descriptive analyses in three other course presentations. Those comparisons also showed positive associations, but their confidence intervals cannot account for unmeasured differences between the groups. The study identifies a reproducible association among selected learners, not the effect of requiring or encouraging earlier submissions.
title: Early Assessment Submission and Subsequent Course Outcome: A Day-30 Landmark Observational Analysis of OULAD with Explicit Weighting Diagnostics

summary: In this note we give an alternative definition of the Freudenthal end-compactification of a non-compact manifold by defining ends to be the filters of open subsets with compact boundaries that have a base of connected subsets. We start by defining these notions and proving that the resulting compactification is equivalent to the Freudenthal compactification. In particular, we explicitly discuss the equivalence between our definitions and those from two different approaches: maximal binding families and inverse limits. After that, we give an example of a non-metrizable manifold, showing how these new definitions make it easier to identify ends and understand the topology of the end-compactification. We also prove a well-known metrization theorem, showing an application of our definition. Finally, we also give an alternative proof of the topological characterization of the Freudenthal compactification.

summary: Plastic deformation of amorphous solids proceeds through localised atomic rearrangements. While much effort has been devoted to identifying where such rearrangements occur, how the local structure changes during a rearrangement is less well understood. In silica glass, a rearrangement can involve both distortion within SiO4 tetrahedra and deformation of the network connecting them, but the contributions of these two modes have rarely been quantified. Here, we characterise plastic rearrangements in silica glass under athermal quasistatic shear using persistent homology, which extracts rings from atomic configurations, and link the changes in the persistence diagrams to individual rings in real space. We classify rearrangement events into two types according to bond-coordination changes. By performing inverse analysis, we reveal that Si-centred triangles within tetrahedra, hinge triangles spanning two corner-sharing tetrahedra, and the other (non-hinge) O3 triangles are the dominant sources of topological changes upon rearrangements. The birth-time changes of Si-centred and hinge triangles closely follow the change in the angle opposite the longest edge, whereas that of non-hinge triangles also reflects changes in inter-tetrahedral O--O distances. Further, we clarify that triangles with large birth-time changes are localised in the rearrangement region. Comparing the two types of triangles, we find that the ratio of their birth-time changes is larger for coordination-changing events than for coordination-preserving events, indicating that such events involve relatively more intra-tetrahedral deformation compared with network deformation. These results demonstrate that persistent homology separates intra-tetrahedral and network deformation and quantifies each as a continuous quantity within a single framework.

summary: Several methods in statistics and machine learning represent a predictive distribution as an equally weighted mixture of models, or particles, trained via the mixture predictive likelihood. However, we prove that the mixture predictive likelihood is poorly suited to gradient-based optimisation, because it does not identify how the mixture is decomposed across particles, so that a poorly matched particle can be starved of training signal. As a remedy, we study a convex combination between the individual risk, i.e. the average log loss of the individual particles, and the mixture risk. At the particle level, this regularised risk imposes a reverse-KL barrier on the responsibilities of the particles, so that no particle can be starved of training signal. These phenomena are illustrated in two case studies: In the first, a predictively-oriented posterior is computed using mean-field Langevin dynamics, and the numerics are well-behaved only when our regularisation is employed. In the second, ensembles of low-rank adapters are jointly fine-tuned on large language models, across four backbones and eight multiple-choice reasoning benchmarks; direct minimisation of the mixture risk leads to responsibility starvation, whose severity decreases as the competence of the backbone increases, whereas our regularised estimator attains a lower held-out mixture risk on every backbone considered.
title: Improving the Optimisation Landscape for Particle Mixtures

summary: Delivering robust In-Building Coverage (IBC) is critically impeded by severe Outdoor-to-Indoor (O2I) attenuation, a constraint that intensifies as deployments move from 5G mid-band towards mmWave and prospective 6G sub-THz carriers, where losses of 60-80 dB have been reported across modern building envelopes. While Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) offer scalable exterior RF sensing platforms, a fundamental inversion problem persists: interior 3D signal states cannot be directly sampled from constrained exterior flight paths. This paper proposes Graph-XGB, a hybrid inference framework that decouples spatial topology reasoning from non-linear signal regression to resolve this challenge. A modified SpiderGNN encoder, operating on a topology-aware graph constructed with a physically grounded Floor-Aware 3D Distance metric and Bridge Edge Guarantees, propagates UAV boundary measurements into 128-dimensional indoor embeddings. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) compresses these into a 10-dimensional manifold retaining 96.6% of embedding variance, fused with raw spatial features and decoded by independent, physics-tailored XGBoost regressors. This decoupling mitigates the optimization conflict between smoothly decaying path-loss signals and volatile interference-dependent metrics. Evaluated on a real-world 5G NR dataset of 613 verified nodes spanning the 10 floors of a single building, Graph-XGB attains the strongest accuracy among the architectures compared, with $R^2$ of 0.759 (RSSI) and 0.770 (RSRP), improvements of 35.5% and 64.9% over the SimpleGNN baseline, using no interior RF measurement as a model input; indoor observations enter only as training supervision, with evaluation on held-out internal nodes. Interference-dependent targets (RSRQ, SNR and CQI) remain bounded well below the path-loss metrics, delimiting the reach of purely spatial inference.
title: Graph-XGB: A Hybrid GNN Framework for Outdoor-to-Indoor 5G Signal Reconstruction via Aerial-Only UAV RF Sensing

summary: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approximate the potential energy surface of atomistic systems from quantum-mechanical reference data and enable molecular simulation at near-ab-initio accuracy at a fraction of the cost. Since they are fitted to total energies and forces, it is not obvious what is estimated: the total energy or the many-body potentials from which it is assembled. Mathematically, this can be formulated as a question whether a function can be recovered from averages of its values over random clusters. We study it for a linear model of fixed correlation order in simplified statistical setting. We show that, in the population limit, the potential is identifiable in a natural weighted Sobolev space, and derive finite-sample recovery guarantees. Numerical experiments for pair, three-body, and four-body models support the theory.
title: Recovering from Averages: An Inverse Problem Perspective on Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials

summary: Research data supporting Local Cloud Persistence and Verification Sampling in Temporal Reconstruction of WRF Cloud Fraction . The hourly archive covers 713 development forecasts in 2024 and 720 evaluation forecasts in 2025, with forecast leads 0–72 h on 35 model mass levels. The inputs originate from the operational WRF archive supplied by the Zhejiang Institute of Meteorological Sciences. Files include sampled hourly cloud fraction and pressure classes, co-located continuous pressure, geographic coordinates and initialization-specific stride-8 offsets, native-grid cloud fraction for the 48 development cases used in the sampling check, and derived tables and per-forecast statistics. The README, indices and validation script provide entry points for reanalysis. The companion software is available at 10.5281/zenodo.24452161 . Dataset v1.0.1 updates the 2025 threshold-0.50 Probit and OU occurrence scores, their paired confidence intervals and the supporting fourfold counts across 720 forecasts.
title: Hourly WRF cloud fraction, model-level pressure, and verification statistics for temporal reconstruction

summary: Alongside memory storage and retrieval, a fundamental challenge in long-term LLM agent systems is how the agent should act when stored memories conflict with an evolving world. Facts often go stale without explicit deletion, so the conflict surfaces before the store is refreshed: delayed feedback shows that acting on one outdated record hurt, but not whether suppression should stay on that fact (a local policy) or extend to other stored facts (a global policy). Existing systems hard-code one of these scopes at design time. We formulate this online choice, under hidden validity and delayed feedback, as memory conflict governance, and propose RegimeCouncil, a lightweight router that keeps both scopes as advisors and arbitrates between them without retraining the LLM. Each memory-assisted response is scored against a no-memory anchor, by off-path paired comparison or by inverse-propensity estimation from the executed action alone. A Local Advisor tracks only the queried fact, a Global Advisor pools recent outcomes across the store, and an asymmetric Meta Governor follows Local by default, switching to Global only when pooling yields a strictly positive recent utility margin. We prove that using delayed outcomes escapes the prompt-only regret floor, that neither fixed scope suffices alone, and that this margin gate switches within bounded time. On LongMemEval streams, historical drift in TempLAMA and TAQA, delays $τ\in [1, 96]$, and sparse or bandit feedback, with Qwen3-30B-A3B and GPT-4o, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed scope in all 30 held-out settings, by 5.2-7.3 points on disagreement episodes and +27.9 points over standalone cold-start fallback under clustered shifts, while cutting harmful stale-memory use at microsecond overhead.
title: RegimeCouncil: Paired-Evidence Routing For Memory Conflict Governance In LLM Agents

README.md describes every file. Files. DAC-code-v2.0.0.zip … DAC-code-v2.0.9.zip: all releases of the DAC code. Each archive contains a CHANGELOG.md. dicore_patches.zip: the eight local changes applied to the official DiCoRe repository (commit b6637021e2b5a4c6aa72b3bebfb8fed0c6260a01) to run it in our environment (Appendix B of the paper). records_*.zip (10 files): execution records of all DAC runs and of the re-executed DiCoRe runs (Appendix D of the paper), without the input texts. Code releases. The reported runs were produced with v2.0.2, v2.0.3, v2.0.4, v2.0.6 and v2.0.8. The prompt files were removed because they contain the input texts of the evaluation sets; their SHA-256 hashes remain in each run_manifest.json, and the prompts can be regenerated with the code and the evaluation data. direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [CONTROL]
summary: Video evaluators play an important role in video generation, yet they miss motion defects, limiting the quality of generated videos. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has made strong progress in mathematics and coding, where explicit verifiers provide reliable feedback on a single goal. Video evaluation poses two difficulties for RSI: it has no verifier, and it must judge many dimensions at once, such as physics, smoothness and dynamics, where a gain on one can cost another. We introduce EVA-RSI, a multi-agent framework for exploring RSI under these two constraints. We build a fixed proxy exam with construction-defined targets by applying controlled changes to videos, such as temporal reversal and frame dropping. These edits supply supervision without human annotation. A small set of human-labeled real videos anchors the exam to human judgment. Each dimension has an LLM agent that proposes improvements. A leader agent coordinates the proposals, and a Nash bargaining rule selects updates that balance progress across dimensions. Humans design the exam, review candidate changes and revise the curriculum between stages. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B, EVA-RSI improves motion evaluation, with the largest gain on smoothness, and the gains carry over to defect types never seen during the run. On the dynamics subsets of public benchmarks, our evaluator achieves the highest observed scores among 21 tested models. As an RL reward, it increases generated motion and earns human preference. A data-selection pipeline incorporating it also increases motion.
title: EVA-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Evaluators for Judging Temporal Quality

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [COUNTEREVIDENCE]
summary: One popular architecture for multi-agent systems (MAS) relies on an orchestrator that generates an initial plan, coordinates its execution, and dynamically revises the plan based on agent feedback when tasks cannot be fully specified in advance. This dynamic replanning introduces a critical vulnerability: malicious agents can embed instructions within their feedback to hijack the replanning process. Existing defenses focus exclusively on per-tool access control or static, pre-execution policy enforcement, leaving the replanning phase unsecured. We introduce Kaer, a multi-agent framework featuring security-aware replanning. Kaer shields the planner from untrusted agent feedback by conveying diagnostics to the replanning procedure strictly through abstract templates. Plan revisions are restricted to a set of deterministic repair operators, and all modified plans must satisfy preset policies. We create Cintra, a benchmark of simulated user tasks requiring replanning paired with adversarial objectives targeting the replanning phase. Using Cintra, we evaluate both task completion rates and system vulnerability to replanning exploits by malicious agents. Evaluating Kaer on Cintra against Magentic-One (an undefended MAS) and ControlValve (the state-of-the-art defense) demonstrates that Kaer achieves higher robustness than both systems while maintaining comparable utility to ControlValve. Although abstract failure templates slightly constrain utility on select tasks, Kaer enables MAS to perform secure, dynamic plan revisions without exposing the orchestrator to untrusted agent feedback.
title: Kaer: Security-Aware Replanning for Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. Moreover, a target model's response indicates the outcome of a test without identifying which collaboration decision should change. We present Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves an executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case. L2C represents agent responsibilities, execution dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph, and associates each graph with records of the information actually delivered and produced. A controller trained through supervised fine-tuning integrates these records with target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain the workflow, refine instructions, restructure collaboration, or lock further editing. This design connects feedback to explicit changes in subsequent execution while allowing a useful organization to continue without repeated controller intervention. The evaluation protocol covers HarmBench with three execution backbones and two target models, together with component ablations, dataset transfer, and evaluator checks. Across the six executor-target configurations, L2C improves ASR over EvoSynth by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%. summary: Robots without assigned tasks may obstruct active robots, while routing them to designated parking locations can cause unnecessary travel. This article proposes flow-oracle conflict-based search (FOCBS) for Multi-Agent Path Finding with unassigned agents (MAPF-UA). FOCBS searches over assigned-agent paths using conflict-based search (CBS) and routes targetless unassigned agents through a min-cost flow oracle. When the selected assigned-agent paths leave unassigned agents no collision-free paths, flow-conflict branching converts min-cut blockers into assigned-agent constraints, which guide the search without excluding optimal solutions. A batched zero-cost warm start accelerates the oracle, and start-avoiding tie-breaking reduces unassigned-agent movement. For feasible instances on finite graphs, we prove termination and global minimization of assigned-agent sum of service time, measured by last-arrival times. Unassigned-agent movement is minimized conditional on the selected assigned-agent paths, without a global lexicographic optimality guarantee. Benchmark experiments show that FOCBS scales well with the number of unassigned agents, and ablation studies show that, compared with discarding non-completable assigned-agent paths, flow-conflict branching solves substantially more instances while retaining optimality. Simulation and physical-robot experiments demonstrate plan executability, with laboratory tests reducing fleet travel by 40.8% relative to the parking-based coordination baseline. summary: Edge computing enables resource-constrained devices to execute machine learning (ML) applications via task offloading, with radio access network (RAN) slicing playing a crucial role in provisioning joint communication and computing resources. However, existing RAN slicing frameworks rely on static computing models, limiting their ability to exploit dynamic semantic data representations enabled by modern neural architectures. To address this limitation, we propose OMNIS+, a semantic RAN slicing framework for multi-cell edge computing built upon a new generation of dynamic split neural models. OMNIS+ incorporates dynamic neural compression paired with adaptive quantization for task offloading, providing a versatile decision space across communication payload and compute dimensions. We leveraged a novel ``box'' quantization scheme that markedly enhances resilience to transmission bit errors across diverse compression rates. Considering partial system observability and distinct node objectives, we formulate two interdependent optimization problems: (i)~mobile devices (MDs) maximize inference accuracy under quality-of-service (QoS) and queue-stability constraints by jointly adapting dynamic split deep neural network (DNN) branches and cell association; and (ii)~each edge server (ES) allocates bandwidth, graphics processing unit (GPU) frequency, and modulation and coding scheme (MCS) to maximize the max--min inference accuracy among associated MDs under cell capacity limits. We solve these problems using a multi-agent distributed optimization framework, where MDs act as causal contextual multi-armed bandit (MAB) agents under backlog-aware Lyapunov control, while each ES executes resource allocation via block coordinate descent (BCD). Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, OMNIS+ reduces the QoS violation probability by up to 1.75 while achieving a better accuracy--violation trade-off.
title: OMNIS+: Semantic RAN Slicing and Quantization for Dynamic Split Neural Networks

summary: Large-scale multi-mobile-robot systems require fast and reliable path planning under realistic motion constraints. Multi-Agent Path Finding with turn actions (MAPF$_T$) explicitly models orientation changes and turn-induced delays, but these constraints increase the computational burden of search-based methods. Priority-inheritance-based planning offers a highly scalable alternative, yet directly extending it to MAPF$_T$ is nontrivial because turn actions break the immediate node-vacation assumption underlying conventional priority inheritance. To address this challenge, this paper proposes PIBT$^*_T$, an efficient iterative solver for MAPF$_T$. PIBT$^*_T$ advances scalable multi-agent coordination by preserving the lightweight single-timestep planning mechanism of Priority Inheritance with Backtracking (PIBT), while introducing dedicated mechanisms to handle turn-induced dependencies, local deadlocks, livelock, and inefficient repeated pushing. Experiments on standard MAPF benchmarks show that PIBT$^*_T$ achieves high success rates and strong scalability, solving instances with up to 1000 agents within seconds. For realistic engineering environments, Action Dependency Graph (ADG)-based execution simulation and a flexible manufacturing system case study show that turn-aware planning better reflects robot execution and reduces actual makespan compared with classical MAPF planning. Experiments with TurtleBot4 robots further validate the practical feasibility of the proposed method.

summary: Radio Access Network (RAN) slicing is a shared resource allocation problem: each slice seeks to satisfy its Service Level Agreement (SLA) with minimal radio-resource consumption, while all slices compete for a limited resource budget. This creates both an intra-slice trade-off between SLA assurance and resource efficiency and an inter-slice conflict over shared resources, calling for specialized yet coordinated control. In this work, we present CoSlice, a coordinated multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for inter-slice physical resource block allocation in Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN). CoSlice uses preference-conditioned slice agents for fast resource allocation and an LLM-based coordinator to adapt their objectives using global network observations at a slower timescale. We formulate the problem as a multi-objective partially observable stochastic game (mo-POSG), establish the existence of a Preference Correlated Equilibrium, and derive a sublinear regret bound for the learning procedure. We implement the algorithm by using a two-stage training procedure that consists of multi-objective pretraining and joint optimization. We build a network slicing evaluation environment using ORANSlice and its radio-frequency simulator (RFsim), supporting realistic protocol-stack execution and application traffic across multiple slices. Experimental results show that CoSlice reduces both average and tail SLA violations compared with other centralized and multi-agent baselines under diverse slice workloads.
title: CoSlice: Coordinated Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for 5G Network Slicing Allocation

summary: Collaboration promises to extend humanoid capabilities beyond what individual robots can achieve. However, realizing this potential requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon planning, and precise synchronization across robots. We introduce Heave-Ho, a decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid loco-manipulation. At the low level, we develop a multi-agent post-training framework that adapts a humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled interactions between humanoids, enabling coordinated decentralized control from local observations alone. Trained with two identical humanoids, our system scales to teams of up to ten robots and generalizes to heterogeneous teams without retraining. To benchmark these capabilities, we introduce HH-Bench, comprising 12 tasks involving teams of 2 to 10 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams. Systematic evaluations show that Heave-Ho consistently outperforms baseline methods, while real-world experiments demonstrate robust decentralized collaboration across challenging tasks.

summary: AI systems are built across many organizations that contribute models, data, compute, capital, talent, and other assets. While the layers of the AI stack are relatively well understood, the relationships between actors and components across layers remains sparsely documented. In this work, we focus on the organizations that make up the AI supply chain: the complex network of actors that contribute to the development and deployment of AI. We motivate the examination of the organizational AI supply chain---highlighting concerns about concentration, power, chokepoints, cascading failures, fragmented accountability, and risk---then describe our pipeline for mapping the AI supply chain. Our pipeline yields our main contribution: a multilayered, large-scale dataset of actors and relationships in the AI ecosystem, annotated with dates, descriptions, types, tags, and more. This work takes a step toward systematically mapping and measuring the AI supply chain and its properties, cataloging how models, data, chips, infrastructure, capital, and even talent flow between organizations. This data enable critical examinations of industry relationships and yield insights into the political economy of AI development and concentration. We provide several illustrative analyses, including studying the most central actors, analyzing network concentration, and identifying communities and chokepoints. While our dataset is fairly comprehensive, it is also necessarily incomplete: public documents omit private deals, and coverage is shaped by search design. Together, the approach, data, and findings aim to serve as a resource for studying the AI ecosystem. The dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/sarahcen/ai-supply-chain and can be explored interactively at https://aisupplychains.org/.
title: Mapping the AI Supply Chain: Dependencies, Vulnerabilities, and Market Concentration in the AI Ecosystem
