summary: This academic curriculum module delivers an analytical, physical, and computational treatment of modern avionics architectures, real-time sensing networks, and deterministic flight computers across commercial, military, and space environments. Key Technical Topics & Curricular Areas Covered: 1. Core Avionics Subsystems: Radio and radar range formulations, monostatic radar equation received power evaluations, GNSS/INS inertial dead reckoning, Fly-by-Wire (FBW) digital flight control, and Health and Usage Monitoring Systems (HUMS). 2. Modern Computational & AI-Era Paradigms: Invariant Extended Kalman Filtering (IEKF) on Lie groups SO(3) and SE_2(3) for singularity-free attitude estimation in GPS-denied environments; Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for synthetic airspeed reconstruction during pitot-static sensor icing; deterministic Time-Triggered Ethernet (TTEthernet / SAE AS6802) in Integrated Modular Avionics (IMA). 3. Airworthiness & Safety Standards: Compliance workflows under RTCA DO-178C (software safety lifecycle), DO-254 (complex electronic hardware), and DO-326A/DO-356A airworthiness cybersecurity threat management. 4. Systems Engineering Trade-offs: Quantitative evaluation of Triple Modular Redundancy (TMR) vs. SWaP-C mass and power budgets, Integrated Modular Avionics vs. federated Line Replaceable Units (LRUs), COTS microprocessors vs. rad-hardened silicon, and databus transport delay impacts on flight control loop phase margin. 5. Communications & Signal Propagation: Free-space path loss (FSPL), RF link budgets, receiver thermal noise floor calculations (kTB), and Doppler frequency shifts in airborne radar. 6. Pedagogical Features: An interactive web-based RF Link Budget and Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) simulator case study, multi-tier conceptual review questions, and step-by-step calculated numerical engineering problems with explicit physical units. Format: Open Educational Resource (OER) prepared for persistent archiving on Zenodo and indexing in MERLOT. Permanent Webpage URL: https://prep4uni.online/stem/physical-technologies/aerospace-and-aeronautical-engineering/avionics/
title: Avionics Explained: Aircraft Systems, Electronics & Flight Control Technologies

summary: This repository accompanies a study comparing canopy-decline prediction and seven- and fourteen-day soil-water onset forecasts across Hungary using multidepth observations, Sentinel-1, MODIS and antecedent weather. It provides scientific Python workflows, aggregate results, publication figures, development protocols and reproducibility instructions. Analyses evaluate false alerts, missed events, calibration, transfer performance and clustered uncertainty under matched inspection budgets. Negative canopy results and uncertain false-alarm improvements are retained. Station-level observations, coordinates, individual predictions and fitted models are excluded because redistribution permissions remain unconfirmed. Included aggregates support numerical checks and selected figure regeneration; full model reconstruction requires authorized inputs. Manuscript-preparation code is excluded.

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [COUNTEREVIDENCE]
summary: People may interpret favorable and unfavorable outcomes differently even when their actual contribution to the relevant activities is broadly comparable. Following a favorable outcome, an individual may emphasize personal ability, effort, judgment, and contribution. Following an unfavorable outcome, the same individual may minimize personal responsibility, redistribute blame, or assign greater explanatory weight to other people, circumstances, or systems. This paper develops the Evolutionary Social-Position Preservation and Outcome- Attribution Asymmetry Theory (ESPOAAT). Its central concern is why the same individual may claim greater personal credit under favorable outcome conditions while reducing personal responsibility and externalizing blame under unfavorable conditions. The framework proposes that this asymmetry may be related to the evolutionary signifi- cance of human social interdependence, reputation, partner selection, competence recognition, prestige, group acceptance, and the potential costs of negative social evaluation. These social conditions are examined alongside self-concept, ego preservation, superiority-related self-investment, cognitive attribution, implicit processing, emotional responses, defensive mechanisms, interpersonal self-presentation, and feedback. The theory identifies nine equally examined mechanisms. These mechanisms cover evo- lutionary social interdependence; reputation and social recognition; competence signaling and social position; blame-burden dilution and social-culpability avoidance; ego and iden- tity preservation; cognitive and implicit attribution; emotional and psychological defense; interpersonal and collective attribution; and cybernetic feedback and cultural reinforcement. The paper distinguishes causal contribution, personal credit, responsibility, and moral blame. It proposes separate operational indices for favorable self-credit amplification, unfa- vorable self-responsibility attenuation, and external blame displacement. It also develops an evolutionary-social payoff framework, testable hypotheses, boundary conditions, and a multi-stage research program. The framework does not assume that all external attributions are defensive, that all individuals behave asymmetrically, or that blame-shifting itself has been established as a direct evolutionary adaptation. Instead, it treats the proposed evolutionary and psychological pathways as distinct but potentially interacting explanations requiring empirical validation. Keywords: evolutionary social psychology; social-position preservation; outcome attribution; self-serving bias; competence signaling; reputation; blame-burden dilution; ego protection; group attribution; social feedback.

title: Evolutionary Social-Position Preservation and Outcome-Attribution Asymmetry Theory

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Dynamic systems operate under limited or constrained capacities. The demands placed on them may exceed their available resources, processing capacity, operational limits, or remaining time. Under such conditions, continued activity may become increasingly difficult, inefficient, or potentially harmful to the wider system. This paper proposes the Threshold-Governed Resource-Preserving Disengagement Theory (TGRPDT), a general conditional framework for examining how a capacity-constrained system changes its response to an ongoing task or objective when continuation becomes insufficiently feasible or disproportionately costly. The central theoretical conflict is between continuation and preservation. The framework proposes that, under specified conditions, a system may reduce its operational intensity, selectively remove lower-priority activities, partially disengage, temporarily suspend an activity, defer its execution, or terminate the objective altogether. The proposed central process is designated the Resource-Preserving Threshold-Response Mechanism (RPTRM). Its stronger complete-abort form is designated the Resource Optimization and Threshold-Driven Abort Mechanism (RO-TAM). A principal behavioral application is the Deadline-Capacity Collision-Induced Task Withdrawal (DCCW) case, represented by an individual encountering an excessive academic workload under a severely restricted preparation deadline. The framework integrates demand-capacity relationships, temporal feasibility, resource reserves, estimated success probability, expected continuation value, partial-output value, and withdrawal decisions. It proposes a generalized overload index, a comparative continuation-disengagement model, a response taxonomy, theoretical propositions, and testable hypotheses. Nineteen research domains are mapped according to their structural, direct, or analogical relationships with the proposed theory. Counterexamples and boundary conditions are included to prevent excessive generalization. The theory is presented as a research framework rather than a proven universal principle. Its independent contribution, mathematical adequacy, predictive performance, and cross-domain applicability require systematic literature comparison, formal derivation, simulation, and empirical validation.
tags: Keywords: Threshold-Governed Response; Resource Preservation; System Disengagement; Demand-Capacity Disparity; Temporal Constraint; Feasibility; Optimal Stopping; Cognitive Overload; Procrastination; Cybernetics; Resource-Constrained Systems; Protective Withdrawal.
title: THE THRESHOLD-GOVERNED RESOURCE-PRESERVING DISENGAGEMENT THEORY (TGRPDT)

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [REVERSE]
summary: A system cannot continue performing every task under every condition. Its ability to continue depends on the demands placed upon it and the resources and capacities available to meet those demands. When the demands imposed upon a system exceed its effective capacity, a mismatch may develop between what is required and what the system can effectively perform. The mismatch may become more serious when available time, energy, information, money, processing capacity, or other necessary resources are limited. This paper proposes the Demand-Capacity Threshold Withdrawal Theory (DCTWT), a cross-domain theoretical framework for examining how constrained systems respond when demands exceed their effective capacity and relevant operational limits are approached or crossed. The central argument is that, under certain conditions, an increasing mismatch between demand and capacity may produce a change in ongoing activity. A system may continue operating, reduce its activity, modify its method, maintain only part of its operation, temporarily suspend an activity, or terminate it entirely. Withdrawal is particularly relevant when continuing the same activity is no longer feasible, is unlikely to produce an effective result, or creates additional pressure on remaining resources. The theory identifies the Threshold-Triggered Activity Withdrawal Mechanism (TTAWM) as its proposed central mechanism. The mechanism connects demand input, capacity limitation, demand-capacity divergence, constraint accumulation, threshold conditions, operational response changes, activity withdrawal, resource consequences, and possible recovery or termination. An illustrative academic case, named Deadline-Capacity Collision-Induced Academic Task Withdrawal (DCC-ATW), is used as the primary human case. The framework also examines potential applications in general systems theory, cybernetics, mathematics, cognitive psychology, behavioral psychology, procrastination studies, decision theory, computer science, artificial intelligence, engineering, biology, information theory, sociology, and organizational management. A general mathematical architecture is proposed using demand, capacity, temporal pressure, resource availability, threshold conditions, response functions, and resource-balance relationships. The manuscript further develops theoretical propositions, testable hypotheses, operational definitions, boundary conditions, alternative explanations, and an empirical validation framework. The central contribution proposed by DCTWT is not that all systems share an identical internal mechanism, but that a common demand-capacity-constraint pattern may help explain certain changes in system activity, including resource-preserving withdrawal, across otherwise different types of systems. The framework remains a proposed theory. Its originality, mathematical consistency, predictive value, and cross-domain generalizability require systematic evaluation and empirical testing. Keywords: Demand-Capacity Conflict; Threshold; Activity Withdrawal; Resource Preservation; System Constraints; System Response; Cognitive Overload; Procrastination; Optimal Stopping; General Systems Theory; Cybernetics; Dynamic Systems.

title: DEMAND-CAPACITY THRESHOLD WITHDRAWAL THEORY

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [COUNTEREVIDENCE]
summary: A system cannot continue performing every task under every condition. Its ability to continue depends on the demands placed upon it and the resources and capacities available to meet those demands. When the demands imposed upon a system exceed its effective capacity, a mismatch may develop between what is required and what the system can effectively perform. The mismatch may become more serious when available time, energy, information, money, processing capacity, or other necessary resources are limited. This paper proposes the Demand-Capacity Threshold Withdrawal Theory (DCTWT), a cross-domain theoretical framework for examining how constrained systems respond when demands exceed their effective capacity and relevant operational limits are approached or crossed. The central argument is that, under certain conditions, an increasing mismatch between demand and capacity may produce a change in ongoing activity. A system may continue operating, reduce its activity, modify its method, maintain only part of its operation, temporarily suspend an activity, or terminate it entirely. Withdrawal is particularly relevant when continuing the same activity is no longer feasible, is unlikely to produce an effective result, or creates additional pressure on remaining resources. The theory identifies the Threshold-Triggered Activity Withdrawal Mechanism (TTAWM) as its proposed central mechanism. The mechanism connects demand input, capacity limitation, demand-capacity divergence, constraint accumulation, threshold conditions, operational response changes, activity withdrawal, resource consequences, and possible recovery or termination. An illustrative academic case, named Deadline-Capacity Collision-Induced Academic Task Withdrawal (DCC-ATW), is used as the primary human case. The framework also examines potential applications in general systems theory, cybernetics, mathematics, cognitive psychology, behavioral psychology, procrastination studies, decision theory, computer science, artificial intelligence, engineering, biology, information theory, sociology, and organizational management. A general mathematical architecture is proposed using demand, capacity, temporal pressure, resource availability, threshold conditions, response functions, and resource-balance relationships. The manuscript further develops theoretical propositions, testable hypotheses, operational definitions, boundary conditions, alternative explanations, and an empirical validation framework. The central contribution proposed by DCTWT is not that all systems share an identical internal mechanism, but that a common demand-capacity-constraint pattern may help explain certain changes in system activity, including resource-preserving withdrawal, across otherwise different types of systems. The framework remains a proposed theory. Its originality, mathematical consistency, predictive value, and cross-domain generalizability require systematic evaluation and empirical testing. summary: This paper proposes the Extremal Input-Response Divergence Theory (EIRDT), a general theoretical framework for examining how a system may respond differently to the excessive presence and extreme absence of the same functional input. The central concern of the theory is not merely that two opposite input conditions can produce different outcomes. Its more specific concern is that, under certain internal and contextual conditions, the direction of a system's response may become opposite to the expected direction of the input. The principal response pattern is termed Input-Response Directional Inversion (IRDI). In its primary relational case, extreme availability may be associated with a reduction in a recipient's perceived attraction, whereas extreme unavailability may, under certain conditions, be associated with increased attraction or mental preoccupation. These are proposed conditional patterns, not deterministic laws. The framework distinguishes input magnitude, internal state, context, processing mechanisms, response variables, temporal effects and feedback. It also distinguishes directional inversion from ordinary nonlinearity, response asymmetry, cross-output divergence, response nullification and other forms of divergent outcomes. A general state-space mathematical architecture is proposed. The architecture includes a formal comparison of high, reference and low input conditions, a conditional definition of IRDI, multidimensional output modelling, temporal dynamics and system-specific equilibrium determination. The paper further develops an eleven-layer theoretical structure, a classification of response patterns, research propositions, testable hypotheses, operational definitions and an empirical validation roadmap. The theory is intended to be applicable beyond interpersonal relationships, provided that a system has identifiable inputs, internal states and measurable outputs. Its applicability to any specific domain must be established independently. No empirical dataset is presented in this paper. The mathematical architecture and theoretical propositions therefore remain subject to formal identification, experimental testing, replication and revision. direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [COUNTEREVIDENCE]
summary: The complete convergence trace of every run of a preregistered blind test of structural attraction in six recent metaheuristics (hippopotamus, black-winged kite, secretary bird, puma, parrot and starfish optimizers). The methods were chosen by a rule frozen before the candidate list was retrieved; predictions about where in the coordinate system each is drawn were registered (osf.io/wc8gm) before any objective function was run on them, and the test that decides them was registered next (osf.io/c4pxz). The optimum of five benchmark functions is moved, together with its search box, to the origin, to points ±c(1,…,1), to mixed-sign points at the same distances and along a sign orbit: 202,500 runs. A box component records where 9,000 runs end on an objective with no structure. The record also holds the re-run of every WOA row of two earlier experiments after an implementation correction (protocol revision R37: the random whale is drawn per coordinate, as in the authors' code): 145,125 runs. The earlier runs stay in 10.5281/zenodo.21986302 and 10.5281/zenodo.24288806. Not summaries: the recorded best-so-far value at every improvement, for every run. README.md specifies the container format byte by byte and shows how to read a run with the Python standard library and numpy. The analysis reports, the fidelity and pilot runs declared in the registration, and the code at the deposit's commit are included.
title: Convergence traces from a preregistered blind test of structural attraction in six metaheuristics, with a corrected re-run of WOA

Five-flagship scientific introduction F171 | Co-Design of 3D Neural Regeneration Scaffolds and Nanomaterials at the Limit Co-Design of 3D Neural Regeneration Scaffolds and Nanomaterials at the Limit asks whether geometry and material co-design can improve neurite guidance error (rad) while remaining within independently defined restrictions. Begin with acellular scaffold; approved culture only separately. The benchmark is optimized conventional neural scaffold, and the competing account is that surface chemistry or selective cell survival explains the difference. The critical evidence is a chemistry and topography matched witness, not a favorable image or internal sensor readout. A future investigation must stop or narrow its claim whenever loss of viability or material containment is observed or cannot be excluded. No biological intervention is specified in this working edition. F172 | Mechanical Compatibility of 4D Flexible Neural Interfaces at the Limit Mechanical Compatibility of 4D Flexible Neural Interfaces at the Limit asks whether strain-matched compliant contact can improve strain mismatch (1) while remaining within independently defined restrictions. Begin with soft tissue phantom and flexible electrode surrogate. The benchmark is optimized static flexible interface, and the competing account is that fixture motion rather than material compliance explains the response. The critical evidence is a local strain and contact witness, not a favorable image or internal sensor readout. A future investigation must stop or narrow its claim whenever contact injury or delamination is observed or cannot be excluded. No biological intervention is specified in this working edition. F173 | Signal Transmission Between Nanoelectrodes and 3D Neural Tissues at the Limit Signal Transmission Between Nanoelectrodes and 3D Neural Tissues at the Limit asks whether impedance and noise calibrated interface can improve signal estimation error (V) while remaining within independently defined restrictions. Begin with saline phantom and synthetic source. The benchmark is optimized conventional microelectrode, and the competing account is that capacitive artifact explains the signal. The critical evidence is a independent calibrated source and artifact witness, not a favorable image or internal sensor readout. A future investigation must stop or narrow its claim whenever charge, heat or tissue limit is observed or cannot be excluded. No biological intervention is specified in this working edition. F174 | Engineered Neuromuscular Junction Models and Functional Reconstruction at the Limit Engineered Neuromuscular Junction Models and Functional Reconstruction at the Limit asks whether aligned neural-muscle model architecture can improve evoked response failure fraction (1) while remaining within independently defined restrictions. Begin with digital response emulator; approved co-culture only separately. The benchmark is optimized conventional separated and coupled model controls, and the competing account is that direct muscle activation explains the response. The critical evidence is a independent source and force-response witness, not a favorable image or internal sensor readout. A future investigation must stop or narrow its claim whenever cell injury or nonphysiological response is observed or cannot be excluded. No biological intervention is specified in this working edition. F175 | Nonclinical Co-Validation of Regenerative Tissues and Brain–Computer Interfaces at the Limit Nonclinical Co-Validation of Regenerative Tissues and Brain–Computer Interfaces at the Limit asks whether hardware-in-loop readout with bounded control can improve false intent-to-response fraction (1) while remaining within independently defined restrictions. Begin with synthetic neural signal emulator and inert hardware-in-loop. The benchmark is optimized classical decoder and conventional interface, and the competing account is that label leakage or device assistance masks response. The critical evidence is a independent label and no-assistance response witness, not a favorable image or internal sensor readout. A future investigation must stop or narrow its claim whenever unauthorized output or tissue injury is observed or cannot be excluded. No biological intervention is specified in this working edition. summary: Run outputs, analysis outputs, and inputs supporting the article STDN-GEN: rapid synthesis of layered critical-material dependency networks for supply-chain sustainability analysis (Communications Sustainability, under review). STDN-GEN builds shallow technology dependency networks that link a technology to its manufacturing components, the materials those components use, and the countries that produce those materials. The deposit covers a benchmark of 180 technologies in microelectronics, biotechnology, and pharmaceuticals, run five times under each reported configuration. stdngen_inputs.zip : technology lists, gold-standard annotations, per-technology canonical vocabularies (two independent passes), material resolution map, World Bank WGI and UNDP HDI inputs. stdngen_runs_raw.zip : one CSV per run (component, material, and country edges with confidences and provenance), debate transcripts, and token-usage logs. stdngen_runs_normalized.zip : runs after per-technology canonical normalization (passes A and B), plus the normalization used in the submitted version for traceability. stdngen_runs_resolved.zip : runs after resolution of generic material labels to compound and elemental forms, with the source of each country share. stdngen_analysis.zip : analysis outputs behind the tables and figures, including the naive baseline, sampling tests, and vocabulary seeding test. stdngen_fig4_source_data.csv (added in version 1.1): source data for Fig. 4, per-technology median pairwise Jaccard for the 60 microelectronics technologies under each condition. See README.md for file naming and SHA256SUMS.txt for checksums. Code: github.com/dads2busy/dpi_stdn_agentic (results produced with commit 8b5b092). Country shares come from USGS commodity statistics where available and are otherwise model-estimated; each row records its source.
title: STDN-GEN: run outputs and analysis data for layered critical-material dependency networks (180 technologies)

summary: PAAMsea is the current form of the PAAM (Pattern Agency on Active Media) set. Version 10.2, 9 November 2026. This core builds, in four layers, a theory of patterns of any physical nature: what a pattern is, how patterns combine, how they are born, divide, fuse and end, and what they cost. Each layer adds one structure to the layer below and states only what that structure buys; no definition, claim or hypothesis of a layer rests on a statement of a higher one. Layers: L0 — fields, symmetry and patterns; L1 — the derivative; L2 — noise; L3 — thermodynamic embedding. The set consists of five documents, each as .tex and .pdf: CORE — mathematics only, in four layers; every statement is proved or cited, with its provenance and the executable checks that test it. LEDGER — the map of subjects and the records that connect observations to the layer and comparison each one tests. STATE — questions, predictions and evidence; the audit of the tools in appendices. CONTEXT — design, decisions, plans and notes; the revision log and the crosswalk from the earlier sets 6.20 and 8.13.1 in appendices. ATLAS — the explanatory companion, in Russian. The archive also holds the build tools (Python and LaTeX sources) and the data the build reads; data kept by the author are identified by their hashes only. The whole set is rebuilt with: python3 tools/paam_build.py --pdf Status of 10.2: 375 statements in the core; 215 executable checks, all passing; 318 records in the ledger. Changes in 10.2 (since 10.0 of 1 November 2026): Core: the title line only; every mathematical file of layers L0–L3 is byte-identical to 10.0. Ledger: seven new primary measurements (E304–E310); E311 and E312 supersede E113 and E162; E313–E318 describe experimental systems. Records E1–E303 are preserved unchanged. State: Q1 restated in terms of the current core; Q41 added; Q33 remains open. Context: work items W9 and W40 closed; notes N48 and N49 added; new work item W54; one crosswalk entry corrected.
title: PAAMsea: Patterns over a sea - a layered mathematical core

summary: AgroNexus-Bench v1.0.0 is a curated, provenance-aware leaf spectroscopy dataset designed to support reproducible research on leaf nitrogen estimation and the evaluation of spectral learning methods under biologically meaningful data partitions. The resource integrates three previously published datasets: citrus leaf VNIR reflectance and laboratory nitrogen measurements, the EcoSIS eight-crop leaf spectra and biochemical traits collection, and SensOFOREST holm oak leaf biochemical and spectral observations. The release contains 895 source-level observation records and 892 spectra , including 886 unique observations eligible for four source-specific nitrogen benchmark tasks: Citrus: 684 composite leaf samples, with 204 spectral bands (397.32–1003.58 nm), direct Dumas nitrogen measurements on a dry-mass basis, and orchard, cultivar, and collection-date metadata. EcoSIS: 187 biochemical trait records, 184 paired spectra across eight crop species, and 178 quality-eligible observations. It provides direct dry-mass nitrogen measurements and an explicitly derived area-based nitrogen variable. SensOFOREST: 24 leaf-age observations nested within 12 physical Quercus ilex trees, with 2,101 spectral bands (400–2500 nm) and direct area-based nitrogen measurements. AgroNexus-Bench preserves source-native spectral axes, original measurement units, biological sampling hierarchies, source identifiers, and transformation provenance. It provides structured metadata, quality and eligibility information, nitrogen target definitions, and fixed evaluation partitions for reproducible within-source analysis and group-aware assessment of distribution shifts. Dry-mass nitrogen concentration and area-based nitrogen are treated as distinct quantities. Derived measurements are explicitly identified, and biological dependencies are preserved to reduce the risk of invalid comparisons and data leakage. The dataset is intended for research in plant spectroscopy, agricultural data science, precision agriculture, and reproducible machine-learning evaluation. It does not introduce new laboratory measurements or establish universal model transferability across crops or sensors. The original datasets, their creators, associated publications, and applicable licenses are individually acknowledged in the accompanying documentation.
title: AgroNexus-Bench: A Curated Leaf Nitrogen Spectral Dataset with Provenance and Reproducible Evaluation Splits

summary: AgroNexus-Bench v1.0.0 is a curated, provenance-aware leaf spectroscopy dataset designed to support reproducible research on leaf nitrogen estimation and the evaluation of spectral learning methods under biologically meaningful data partitions. The resource integrates three previously published datasets: citrus leaf VNIR reflectance and laboratory nitrogen measurements, the EcoSIS eight-crop leaf spectra and biochemical traits collection, and SensOFOREST holm oak leaf biochemical and spectral observations. The release contains 895 source-level observation records and 892 spectra , including 886 unique observations eligible for four source-specific nitrogen benchmark tasks: Citrus: 684 composite leaf samples, with 204 spectral bands (397.32–1003.58 nm), direct Dumas nitrogen measurements on a dry-mass basis, and orchard, cultivar, and collection-date metadata. EcoSIS: 187 biochemical trait records, 184 paired spectra across eight crop species, and 178 quality-eligible observations. It provides direct dry-mass nitrogen measurements and an explicitly derived area-based nitrogen variable. SensOFOREST: 24 leaf-age observations nested within 12 physical Quercus ilex trees, with 2,101 spectral bands (400–2500 nm) and direct area-based nitrogen measurements. AgroNexus-Bench preserves source-native spectral axes, original measurement units, biological sampling hierarchies, source identifiers, and transformation provenance. It provides structured metadata, quality and eligibility information, nitrogen target definitions, and fixed evaluation partitions for reproducible within-source analysis and group-aware assessment of distribution shifts. Dry-mass nitrogen concentration and area-based nitrogen are treated as distinct quantities. Derived measurements are explicitly identified, and biological dependencies are preserved to reduce the risk of invalid comparisons and data leakage. The dataset is intended for research in plant spectroscopy, agricultural data science, precision agriculture, and reproducible machine-learning evaluation. It does not introduce new laboratory measurements or establish universal model transferability across crops or sensors. The original datasets, their creators, associated publications, and applicable licenses are individually acknowledged in the accompanying documentation.

summary: HaldaneAudit is a curated dataset and reproducible workflow for comparing equilibrium constants calculated from reversible enzyme kinetics using the Haldane relation with published experimental or evaluated equilibrium references. Resource release 2.0.2 contains 21 curated enzyme-reaction records, including 16 uni–uni and five bi–bi reactions. Each record documents the kinetic measurements, reaction mechanism, experimental conditions, equilibrium comparator, source provenance, evidence assessment, and associated reaction identifiers. The resource reports the signed logarithmic difference between the kinetic and reference equilibrium estimates, its fold magnitude, and an energy-scaled representation. Eighteen of the 21 central estimates differ from their selected references by no more than twofold; three exceed that descriptive threshold. These differences are not interpreted as definitive errors in the kinetic measurements because experimental conditions and uncertainty information are incompletely documented for some records. This release contains two complementary archives: 1. HaldaneAudit_Data_and_Code_v2.0.2.zip The canonical research archive contains the 21-record dataset, experimental-condition and provenance tables, comparator-sensitivity analysis, evidence assessments, candidate tracker, reaction mappings, validation scripts, source documentation, and reproducibility materials. Release 2.0.2 corrects the reported phosphoglucose-isomerase kinetic temperature and ionic-strength status, clarifies the aspartate-aminotransferase rounding convention, and expands the source-screening tracker to 77 entries. It also documents the November 2026 SABIO-RK Export API recheck, including its aggregate results and preservation limitations. 2. HaldaneAudit_GUI_v0.1.0.zip A companion Streamlit graphical interface supports source-assisted preparation of additional HaldaneAudit records. Users can retrieve bibliographic information through DOI lookup, upload and review PDFs, examine extracted kinetic tables, enter experimental conditions and equilibrium references, assess evidence criteria, and export structured JSON screening drafts. The software also supports importing drafts into isolated working datasets without modifying the original 21-record scientific release. New records require separate scientific review before incorporation into a future published resource version. The graphical-interface archive includes editable source tables synchronized with resource release 2.0.2, installation instructions, example inputs, and automated tests. The resource and graphical interface are freely available for research and reuse. Python software is distributed under the MIT License, while curated data and documentation are distributed under CC BY 4.0. Third-party database content remains subject to its original terms. An earlier version of the associated manuscript is available at arXiv:2607.02784. The present release supports the revised manuscript, "HaldaneAudit: a curated resource for comparing enzyme kinetics with equilibrium data".

Five flagship studies F181 · Autonomous Component Replacement in 3D Manufacturing Equipment at the Limit Primary endpoint: replacement failure fraction (1). Minimum prototype: deenergized modular printer mockup. Strong comparator: optimized skilled manual maintenance. Independent stop: unsafe energization or misassembly. F182 · Micro–Nanorobotic Internal Maintenance of Manufacturing Equipment at the Limit Primary endpoint: unresolved internal fault fraction (1). Minimum prototype: deenergized transparent equipment mockup. Strong comparator: optimized preventive maintenance and manual service. Independent stop: tool entrapment or energy isolation breach. F183 · Predictive Equipment Health and Autonomous Maintenance at the Limit Primary endpoint: missed upcoming failure fraction (1). Minimum prototype: historical or fault-injected equipment data. Strong comparator: optimized scheduled maintenance and simple thresholds. Independent stop: unsafe missed alarm. F184 · Autonomous Production Capacity Reconfiguration in Modular Factories at the Limit Primary endpoint: qualified throughput deficit (units/s). Minimum prototype: discrete-event line plus inert module mockup. Strong comparator: optimized fixed modular line or conventional scheduler. Independent stop: unsafe transition or unqualified production. F185 · Energy Supply and Long-Term Operational Resilience of Self-Repairing Factories at the Limit Primary endpoint: unserved critical energy (J). Minimum prototype: bounded low-power factory emulator. Strong comparator: optimized conventional backup and preventive repair. Independent stop: critical power loss or unsafe restart. Zenodo research description Can a manufacturing system restore its own qualified service without confusing apparent recovery with evidence of a safe repair? Five coupled research programs distinguish component replacement, verified internal maintenance, prospective failure detection, sustained qualified throughput and unserved critical energy. Compare optimized skilled maintenance, conventional scheduling and backup strategies at matched time, staff, workload, reserve and equipment budgets. Preserve failed attempts, unreturned tools, missed alarms, rejected output and deferred critical demand. direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [CONTROL]
summary: Choosing a feedback controller after calibrating its uncertainty can invalidate a guarantee established for each fixed candidate. We study common-disturbance replay as a way to calibrate a reusable controller library jointly. A maximum over complete normalized state-and-input responses yields one finite-sample envelope that survives later controller and constraint selection. We give an exact tolerance extension, a matched-shape dominance result over disturbance-first boxes, and a finite-policy formulation for nonlinear dynamics. Experiments comprise 3,000 independent training–calibration–test repetitions across three linear plants and nonlinear lane keeping with steering lag and saturation. With 64 candidates and 159 calibration episodes, joint calibration achieves 89.90 percent simultaneous coverage in the linear benchmark and 89.94 percent in the nonlinear benchmark, against a 90 percent target; separate calibration achieves 74.88 and 70.90 percent. With 639 episodes, linear-library mean margins are 55.30 percent smaller than for the tested Bonferroni method. The stronger objective has a cost: direct physical-risk testing enables more motion in a narrow corridor, and a one-percent risk target forces substantial abstention at longer horizons. Calibrating an incorrect steering model reduces nonlinear library coverage to 63.80 percent despite high physical constraint satisfaction. These findings identify when joint envelopes justify their conservatism and distinguish selection flexibility from physical safety, model fidelity, and repeated-deployment reliability.
title: Selection-Safe Controller Calibration

summary: Contemporary institutions and frontier artificial intelligence systems optimize overwhelmingly for forward synthesis (I): generating plausible mathematical proofs, compliance frameworks, diplomatic communiqués, and synthetic media at near-zero marginal cost. When forward generation becomes abundant and opaque, surface fluency loses discriminatory value while systemic fragility accumulates beneath unverified abstractions. True technical, scientific, and strategic progress now belongs to backward causal reconstruction (C → I)—the disciplined reverse engineering of finished artifacts, physical side-channels, boundary resistance, and empirical footprints back to their underlying generative mechanisms. Anchored in the Three Starrwood Axioms, this monograph demonstrates why working backward from immutable physical constraints is the decisive methodology across formal mathematics, cybersecurity, post-CMOS hardware physics, silicon forensics, and geopolitical strategy.
title: Why Thinking Backward Is Moving Forward

All models are synthetic, not human, biological or clinical findings. Synthetic signals or authorized offline records; human or clinical research requires independent approval. F003 · Temporal Causal Chain from Intention Formation to Movement Initiation at the Limit Primary endpoint: event-delay MAE (s). Minimum prototype: timestamped cue/EMG simulator. Strong comparator: reaction-time model with anticipatory covariates. Independent stop: unsynchronized timestamps. F004 · Sustained Volitional Training and Neural Network Reorganization at the Limit Primary endpoint: test-retest-adjusted connectivity change error (1). Minimum prototype: longitudinal synthetic connectivity graphs. Strong comparator: contact-matched cognitive task. Independent stop: unstable connectivity estimate. F005 · Observability and Identifiability Limits of Autonomous Volition at the Limit Primary endpoint: latent-state recovery RMSE (1). Minimum prototype: two-state neural simulator. Strong comparator: behavior-only latent model. Independent stop: nonidentifiable state.     Zenodo research description Can calibrated neural, autonomic and behavioral signals distinguish preparation, reported effort, observed motor onset, longitudinal network changes and the identifiable portion of a latent model? Five coupled prospective research programs begin with a leaky accumulator, respiratory-adjusted cardiac inference, shared-clock event reconstruction, test-retest-adjusted connectivity and state-space observability. Compare stochastic thresholds, respiration-adjusted regression, anticipatory reaction-time models, contact-matched cognitive tasks and behavior-only inference. Preserve no-event trials, sensor dropout, rival-only cases and unresolved estimates. Eastern philosophical inquiry motivates operational questions, never an assumption that volition is a measurable field or that neural signals settle metaphysical freedom. summary: The work continues the geometric model of the distribution of primes [2] and the work “The Number Arrow and the Line 1/2” [1]. The geometric formula for the number of odd composites up to p², N(p) = 1 + 3(p − 1)(p − 3)/8, is treated as the first level of a ladder in which the scale is squared at each step: 5² → 5⁴ → 5⁸ → 5¹⁶. It is shown that this formula is the best quadratic formula for the level up to 5⁴: it is exact everywhere except for one compensating pair of misses (p = 15 and p = 17). The quadratic lattice of a level holds up to the basis 7 inclusive and breaks down right after it. The error of the formula splits into two superimposed tables: a smooth level correction and an oscillation which, in the explicit formula, is a sum of cosines over the zeros of the zeta function. The main result is a law of levels, checked on exact values of π(x) up to 3³² ≈ 1.9 · 10¹⁵: when the scale is squared, the relative error of the prime count is squared, and the error itself is inverse to the linear scale p = √x obtained from the difference of squares: ε · p stays of order one at all checked steps. The law holding at all steps is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis (von Koch, 1901). The author puts forward the hypothesis that the self-similarity of the ladder may become a route to its proof: for this one must show that the step structure itself does not allow ε · p to grow faster than a power of the logarithm. This step is named but not taken. The method may become the basis for an exact count of prime density by levels without the exponential and the logarithm in the level formula. Section 7 gives a geometric reading for a reader without mathematical training: why the basis of the model is 2, 3, 5, 7, how the seam 8–9 links the linear and the quadratic levels, why the centres of the seam differ by exactly ¼ and how π arises from all the differences together, where zero is on the arrow and why the whole arrow projects into one circle. The similarity with the construction of the Birth of Dimensions model is shown. Section 8 shows that the accumulated mismatch over the seams is Euler's sine at one half ( π ), while accumulation over the primes gives γ (Mertens); that the error of the prime count at a step is of the order of the square root of the mismatch of the frame; and that the transfer of the observer changes nothing if and only if all zeros lie on the axis 1/2 — this is the Hilbert — Pólya programme. Each seam is a right triangle in a circle: the centre along the line is the radius, the centre on the circle the cosine, the hole the sine, and sin² + cos² = 1. The missing step is also written as a statement about positivity: from Mertens' square 2(1 + cos θ )², which pushes the zeros away from 1, to the square of Weil's energy, which must hold them on ½ and forbid pairs of zeros on opposite sides of the circle. direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [COUNTEREVIDENCE]
summary: A phase-only spatial light modulator (SLM) can form hundreds to thousands of optical traps at once. The largest published neutral-atom array holds 6,100 atoms with a trap-depth spread of 11.4 percent. DinHot is an open studio that runs 24 methods (19 published ones and 5 proposed here) on the same task, with the same seeds and metrics, on a scalar Fourier model with a device model. The report gives twelve data contracts, every method with its equations, 14 cases and 1404 benchmark rows. The benchmark gives every method a deadline of 1 s; a row whose median wall clock exceeds 1.5 times it (3 of 210 rows) is over budget and is never a best or a win. A cell is a win only with five seeds on each side, disjoint interquartile ranges and a gap of 0.01 percentage points: on the ideal device the published methods win 0 and the proposed ones 2 of 8 geometries (those of the efficiency-uniformity continuation), and on a crosstalk device 1 against 2 of 7 (those of the device-aware conjugate-gradient refinement, the device model with a weighted-GS warm start, which the warm-started loss of Schroff et al. matches), the other cells tying. Over 9 baked cases, phase-fixed weighted Gerchberg-Saxton leaves a median spread of 0.38 percent against 17 percent for plain Gerchberg-Saxton. The aberration-robust hologram meets a narrowed criterion (a median ratio of 1.439 over 10 seeds), the continuation is not a Pareto front, the learned warm start is refuted by its control and is out of the benchmark, and the device-aware refinement is a negative result. A three-plane network beats its baseline at equal wall clock on all 162 held-out volumes (median accuracy ratio 1.140). The model is simulated, not a calibrated instrument. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CEFOP_DinHot . Interactive studio: https://dinhot.fasl-work.com .
title: DinHot: A Holographic Optical Trap Studio That Compares Hologram Methods at a One-Second Deadline on a Device Model, Where Most Benchmark Cells Tie

summary: Inputs, reference data and results of the slab analyses reported in the article "A secant-stiffness method using precomputed moment-curvature relationships for nonlinear finite element analysis of reinforced concrete slabs" (Engineering Structures, under review) and in its supplementary material. The dataset covers four slab tests (the McNeice slab, slab A1 of Jain and Kennedy, and slabs S1 and S3 of Duddeck et al.), four slabs compared with a layered shell model in Abaqus/CAE 2025 (a slab with openings and mixed supports, a square orthotropic slab, a clamped slab with asymmetric reinforcement and a slab clamped on two adjacent edges) and two circular slabs. It contains the ANSELCA 1.1 input files of the ten slabs, the Abaqus input files, the digitized test curves, the load-displacement curves of both models and the metrics reported in the article. The analyses were run with ANSELCA 1.1.0 (see Related works), whose folder Examples has a script for each slab. See README.md for the folder structure, how to reproduce the analyses and the file formats. This record supersedes the dataset of the submitted version of the article (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20173476).
title: Validation dataset for: A secant-stiffness method using precomputed moment-curvature relationships for nonlinear finite element analysis of reinforced concrete slabs

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Version 2. Coded dataset and analysis code reproducing every analysis in the revised article on the visibility of sustainability and the Sustainable Development Goals in research on experiential and community-engaged pedagogies in entrepreneurship education. The final corpus contains 574 articles (Scopus and Web of Science, 1991–2024; search of 28 July 2025), each coded for sustainability, explicit SDG reference, community engagement, social entrepreneurship, employability and experiential learning, with narrow dictionary variants. Two sensitivity corpora rebuilt from archived exports (596 unscreened, 515 rule-screened) are also included, together with a validation sample of 70 records coded independently by two authors (each coder's codes and the consensus), comparator counts, thematic-map and cohesion outputs. Running python verify_v2.py reproduces the main statistics from the CSV files alone. Raw bibliographic records are not redistributed under the source databases' terms of use; DOIs allow independent retrieval. Version 1 used a separately rebuilt corpus of 596 records for the term-level analysis only and is superseded by this version. See README.md.
title: Replication package: Visibility of sustainability and the Sustainable Development Goals in experiential and community-engaged entrepreneurship education research (1991–2024)

summary: Replication data and code for the PETs4DeFi study of issuer disclosure and the work required to hide it in a cached DeFi eligibility check. The study replays 9,832 primary Aave v3 paths over 58 observed dates (8 September to 4 November 2026 UTC) against each of two observed EAS revocation schedules on Base. Issuer affiliations are counterfactual. The ZIP contains aggregate table inputs, four vector figures, a reproducible plotting script, source checksums and ten independent synthetic validation runs per size for four and 64 issuers. It excludes individual wallet paths and address lists. The paired fee estimates apply to holder access and exclude registry publication and settlement. Frozen GitHub release: https://github.com/KuznetsovKarazin/zksnark-benchmark/releases/tag/econ08-jisa-v1 (commit 45ead683d0cd6cc35c28248233e942ff8157cdb0). The repository code retains its MIT license; original research documentation and aggregate results are provided under CC BY 4.0, and upstream material retains its original terms. Funding: PETs4DeFi, Horizon Europe grant agreement 101308999.

summary: Version 5 (November 2026). Adds the files that reproduce the checks added in the second-round revision of the paper: confidence intervals with HC3 checks, the facet decomposition for all nine exposure measures, additional cognitive-complexity controls, a supervisory-authority control, and correlations among the exposure measures. Corrects the replication protocol (step 40 and the recorded results in Sections 8.0 to 8.2). Redraws Figures S1 and S2. Updates comments and labels in the main analysis script. No data file changed. See the README. Version 4 (18 September 2026). Restores the complete file set: Version 3 was published with only the three new functional-form files and omitted the thirteen carried-forward data and code files. Version 4 contains all sixteen files and fully supersedes Versions 2 and 3. No content changed. Version 3 (14 September 2026). Adds the functional-form analysis introduced in the revised manuscript (Table 9), prepared in response to peer review. No data file changed. The added script and results table compare the published additive index with a strict multiplicative reconstruction, test the accountability × uncertainty interaction, and apply a Bonferroni multiplicity check across the nine exposure measures. The multiplicative index correlates 0.96 with the published additive index and reproduces the entire results table (all eight confirming measures negative, p < 1e-6), and no consistent interaction is detectable at the occupation level: the paper's conclusions are invariant to the functional form of the index. Version 2 (1 September 2026). An internal audit identified a sign-coding error in one of the ten Judgment Cost Index items in Version 1: O NET element 4.C.3.b.8 — titled "Structured versus Unstructured Work" in earlier O NET releases and "Determine Tasks, Priorities and Goals" in release 29.3 — is measured on a freedom-anchored scale and already runs in the theorized direction; Version 1 applied a reverse-coding this scale does not require, inverting that single item. Version 2 corrects the item, rebuilds the index and uncertainty sub-score, and regenerates every derived output. The central result is unchanged: all eight confirming measures remain negative and significant at p < .001, with modest attenuation. The index's internal consistency improves (ten-item alpha 0.72 to 0.83), and the facet decomposition changes in character, with accountability carrying the index's independent effect. The corrected pipeline was validated by running the identical analysis script on the v1 and v2 data, so every difference between versions is attributable solely to this correction. Do not use the Version 1 files for new analyses; they are retained in the version history for the integrity of the record. Replication data and analysis code for Judgment Cost Theory: The Accountable Bearing of Judgment in an Age of Cheap Prediction (West & Cosimano, 2026; SSRN preprint: https://ssrn.com/abstract=6992679 ). The study develops and validates the Judgment Cost Index (JCI), an occupational measure of judgment cost — the burden of making and owning an accountable decision under irreducible uncertainty — constructed from ten O*NET 29.3 descriptors spanning two facets, accountability for outcomes and irreducible uncertainty. The index is related to nine independent measures of occupational AI exposure across 763 six-digit SOC-2018 occupations in hierarchical regressions controlling for cognitive complexity, routineness, education, and wage. Across eight of the nine measures, including all five generative-AI-era indices, higher judgment cost predicts significantly lower AI exposure beyond the controls; the result survives an eight-part robustness battery, 930 alternative constructions of the index, and factor-score weighting. This deposit contains the redistributable analysis dataset (constructed index, sub-scores, controls, employment, and wages for 763 occupations), item-level z

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Decentralized multi-agent LLM systems enable independently administered agents, each with its own operator, model, memory, and configuration, to collaborate on complex tasks without centralized coordination. Agents autonomously decompose tasks, execute subtasks and delegate remaining work to peers, enabling scalability and eliminating single points of failure. However, decentralization also introduces significant security challenges, as no single entity has complete visibility into task execution or the authority to enforce correct behavior across agents. In this paper, we systematize threats from malicious agents in decentralized multi-agent systems and propose mitigation techniques. We first design and evaluate attacks against integrity, availability, and confidentiality, demonstrating that a single malicious agent can cause up to 100% task failure, inflate token consumption and runtime by up to 7.7x and 3.2x, respectively, and exfiltrate up to 94% of relevant prior tasks from benign agents. We then present a cryptographic protocol that produces an irrefutable verified execution trace of every action taken in the system and develop an auditor that analyzes these traces to detect and attribute malicious behavior. Evaluations on HiddenBench using gpt-6.1-sol and Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 show that our protocol incurs negligible latency overhead, while the auditor detects and correctly attributes 98% of attacks, including those that comply with the protocol.
title: Attacks and Defenses in Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems with Hop-by-Hop Task Decomposition and Delegation

summary: Decentralized multi-agent LLM systems enable independently administered agents, each with its own operator, model, memory, and configuration, to collaborate on complex tasks without centralized coordination. summary: Every move in a robot team changes the world in which its teammates must act. Coordinated manipulation therefore calls for predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly create. We introduce MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample. Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention, while preserving a separate control interface for each robot. MAWAM achieves the highest success on all three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover), with 67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA trained on the same demonstrations and cameras. In simulation, MAWAM reaches 90.3% mean success on eight tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations show that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control: without attention, a four-arm relay falls from 95.0% to 39.0%, and without this supervision, Place Food falls from 78.0% to 47.0%.
title: MAWAM: A Multi-Agent World-Action Model for Coordinated Manipulation

summary: Large language models (LLMs) support scientific research, but some of that assistance can also undermine research integrity. Existing safety evaluations in science often measure whether models refuse misconduct requests, but rarely explain whether they even recognize the problem or why they comply. We investigate this gap across 8 LLMs using SciIntBench, an existing benchmark of 1,350 prompts about scientific research integrity. We examine the reasons behind compliance in four steps. First, when asked directly whether fulfilling a request would involve misconduct, models overwhelmingly identify such requests, even in the Most Covert cases (91%), while they refuse to carry out the request in only 34% of cases. Second, we examine which request characteristics are associated with refusal using features that capture how the request is framed, how much the assistant has been told about what it is helping to hide, and how the goal and the user's stake are stated, among others. Third, we estimate that the most significant effect was to rephrase requests as questions about permissibility rather than instructions, which increased refusal from 52% to 88%. Finally, we test two system-prompt fixes: asking models to assess the request before responding and reminding them of responsible conduct of research principles. These changes increase refusal rates on adversarial requests from 58% to 87% and 86%, respectively. Our findings show that models recognize wrongful requests but still help users violate integrity. Understanding why these failures occur and testing ways to reduce them offer promising paths toward more trustworthy AI for science.
title: Why Do LLMs Help with Scientific Misconduct Requests and What to Do About It?: Increasing the Trustworthiness of AI for Science

summary: Scientific discovery requires revisiting the hypotheses in light of new evidence and identifying promising directions beyond those already explored. However, research agents often make claims that are not supported by their observations, explore a narrow hypothesis space, and retain beliefs despite recognizing conflicting evidence. These failures motivate the search for an explicit epistemic state that captures both beliefs about existing hypotheses and directions for further exploration. To this end, we propose Epistemic Compass (EpiCompass), a plug-and-play scaffold that maintains this state through an epistemic tree linking hypotheses, evidence, beliefs, and revisions. As an investigation progresses, EpiCompass reassesses the hypotheses explored against accumulated evidence and uses unresolved conflicts and unexplored directions to guide hypothesis generation. It selects candidates by anticipated epistemic gain, accounting for both refinement of existing hypotheses and expansion of the hypothesis space, and verifies the final conclusion against the accumulated evidence. Experimental results across three scientific discovery benchmarks and three LLM backbones demonstrate that EpiCompass consistently outperforms baselines, with further analyses showing reductions in errors of unsupported claims and failures to revise beliefs.
title: Steering Automated Scientific Discovery via Audited Epistemic Exploration

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [COUNTEREVIDENCE]
summary: Long event streams require identifying each change and applying the changes in order. We train a selector on a frozen language model to read each transition. With API-only access, we ask the model to list the transitions. An external integer register composes them in order. A confidence rule can flag uncertain updates or retain several candidates. We study products of permutations of five items, a task that fixed-depth, log-precision transformers cannot solve on all input lengths under the standard conjecture that $\mathrm{TC}^0 \ne \mathrm{NC}^1$. On two-event windows, a 27B model answered 3 of 100 correctly without visible reasoning and 96 of 100 when it generated intermediate steps. A frozen 0.8B model with a trained selector read every event in 299 of 299 windows of 43,687 events each. The same package passed 298 of 299 new windows on a fresh machine, missing the target of 0.99 for the one-sided 95% lower confidence bound. A separate follow-up sized to allow one failure yielded 472 of 473. On 1,000-event room-swap documents, three of ten models solved all five documents by reasoning alone. All seven models tested both ways at this length solved all five with extraction and the register, with no chain of thought requested. With concurrent extraction, median wall-clock time fell from 136.1 to 10.4 s for Sonnet 5.5 and from 313.5 to 28.0 s for GPT-6.1 Sol. At fixed per-token rates, mean cost per document fell by 55% for Sonnet 5.5 and 44% for GPT-6.1 Sol. A regular expression with an executor also solved all 15 fixed-format documents. On 500 free-form issue-tracker comments, a separately adapted 4B reader identified the recorded value in 68.8% of cases, compared with 61.0% for a frequency baseline fitted on the same training projects.
title: Learning to Read Events for Exact State Tracking with Frozen Language Models

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Simulated manipulation benchmarks measure policy performance using hand-written success checkers that label each episode as a success or failure. Passing an expert demonstration shows that a checker accepts one way of completing the task. Learned policies, however, may stop after partial progress or complete the task in a different way. A checker may then accept an incomplete execution (phantom success) or reject an execution that satisfies the instruction (silent failure). In this paper, we introduce SimAudit, an LLM-based pipeline that audits success checkers against task instructions. SimAudit analyzes the instruction and checker code to identify scenarios where the two may disagree, recreates those scenarios in simulation, and runs the original checker. Multi-view renderings are then used to verify whether the observed behavior satisfies the instruction. Across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and RoboDojo, 183 simulated test cases produced the predicted checker verdict. Visual verification and deduplication yielded 61 distinct defects across 49 tasks, including 40 phantom successes and 21 silent failures. Most defects in RoboCasa365 accepted incomplete executions, most in RoboDojo rejected valid executions, and both error types were common in RoboTwin 2.0. These findings suggest that validating success checkers requires testing both incomplete executions and valid alternatives to expert demonstrations, and motivate more rigorous evaluation protocols for future benchmarks.
title: Phantom Success, Silent Failure: Auditing the Success Checkers of Simulated Manipulation Benchmarks

summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are increasingly integrated into self-driving laboratories (SDLs) to plan experiments and interpret results. However, analytical reasoning alone does not make a laboratory autonomous: autonomy in an SDL is achievable only when the agent can be trusted to act on physical hardware unsupervised and knows when to defer to a human. Here, we present an architecture that integrates an agent at the Analyze-Design interface of the Design-Make-Test-Analyze (DMTA) cycle, enabling agent-driven measurement selection and data interpretation while ensuring that state-changing operations are authorized, validated, and auditable. We demonstrate this architecture on a liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) instrument in an oxidant-screening campaign for synthesizing an organic dye. Within human-defined campaign limits, the agent submitted measurement jobs, interpreted mass spectrometry (MS) and diode-array detection (DAD) data, flagged failed experiments, and produced an oxidant ranking. This ranking matched that obtained from scripted peak integration, and organic chemists confirmed the agent's spectral interpretations and failure assignments. In a simulated environment that replays the archived LC-MS data, where the agent chose which wells to inject under varying injection limits, it measured the highest-yielding condition at about its seventh injection, against 14.5 on average for a random order, and identified it in every campaign with a limit of eight or more injections. An agent can therefore close the analysis-to-design gap while its actions stay bounded and verifiable, which is a step toward greater autonomy for SDLs.
title: Closing the Analyze-to-Design Gap: An Authorization-Bounded Agent for Self-Driving Laboratories

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [COUNTEREVIDENCE]
summary: Model merging combines separately fine-tuned models by adding their task vectors to a shared backbone. Interference is typically assessed only after constructing and evaluating a candidate merge, making coefficient search expensive. We show that a first-order directional derivative of task A's outputs along task B's vector can predict interference, but only when evaluated at the appropriate model. At the receiver model, this derivative forecasts nearby merges per task and per example, halves the accuracy error of a no-change baseline, and identifies most examples whose predictions flip. For full multi-task merges, a single evaluation is insufficient; two evaluations along the merge path are needed. At the shared pretrained backbone, however, the derivative is nearly orthogonal to realized changes in our vision experiments and only partly predictive in LoRA language-model pilots. Controls link this failure to displacement along the receiver's own task vector, not simply parameter distance; the mismatch appears within the first few dozen fine-tuning steps. Freezing receiver-local responses produces a surrogate affine in the merge coefficients. We use it to construct LR-Merge, a label-free correction that optimizes coefficients through convex teacher matching on unlabeled probes, without backpropagation through merged networks. LR-Merge improves all tested closed-form, isotropic, and sparsified base mergers, with gains generally increasing as more tasks are merged. Using pretrained rather than receiver-local responses instead degrades the base merge. LR-Merge matches exact teacher matching through a merged network, which takes roughly three times longer to converge and performs similarly at an equal compute budget. Once built, the surrogate answers new coefficient and task-subset queries in seconds.
title: Watch Where You Linearize: Predicting and Correcting Model-Merging Interference

summary: This dataset and code package contains the numerical source data and reproducibility materials supporting the manuscript “A Memory-Information Window in Finite-Duration Quantum Control.” The deposited materials include exact stationary Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) trajectory calculations, single- and two-qubit Pauli-transfer-matrix (PTM) process data, logarithmic process derivatives, environmental-parameter identifiability metrics, pulse-history comparisons, commuting-control null tests, exact-OU/TCL2 benchmarks, numerical-convergence and complete-positivity analyses, measurement-compression calculations, hidden-case reconstruction results, and gate-duration scaling data. The dimensionless parameters are defined as λ=σtg\lambda=\sigma t_g and rc=τc/tgr_c=\tau_c/t_g , where σ\sigma is the stationary standard deviation of the OU stochastic field, τc\tau_c is its correlation time, and tgt_g is the gate duration. The deposited data support the analysis of short-memory integrated-noise degeneracy, the intermediate memory-information window, long-memory quasi-static suppression of correlation-time information, and the distinction between commuting and noncommuting coherent controls. The archive contains source data underlying the main and Supplementary figures, numerical parameter settings, available random-seed information, and custom code used for the reported calculations. It also includes data for the consistently normalized nested measurement hierarchy used to compare compressed observables with the full informative PTM. The package is intended to support independent inspection and reproduction of the numerical results reported in the manuscript and its Supplementary Information.
title: A Memory-Information Window in Finite-Duration Quantum Control: Numerical Data and Reproducibility Package

summary: Homomorphic encryption enables control computations to be outsourced to a third-party cloud server without disclosing measurements or controller parameters. Applying existing encrypted linear controllers to nonlinear plants requires a compatible representation of the plant dynamics. This paper presents Homomorphically Encrypted Koopman-Based Control (HEK-Control), which connects nonlinear plants to encrypted linear computations through Koopman lifting. A trusted plant-side client evaluates nonlinear functions of the measured state, and a linear predictor identified in these coordinates supports conventional controller design. The resulting control laws retain the server's encrypted linear operations. We demonstrate the framework using state feedback based on linear quadratic regulation and input-constrained model predictive control. Closed-loop simulations with the Cheon--Kim--Kim--Song encryption scheme show close agreement with unencrypted computations. Additional unencrypted simulations compare regulation under input constraints across a common set of controller designs. For a continuous stirred-tank reactor, Koopman lifting supports regulation at input bounds not handled by the tested controllers designed directly in the original state coordinates. Tests of encrypted computations also show that packing multiple values into each ciphertext reduces computation time and communication volume. These results clarify how existing encrypted linear computations can serve nonlinear plants.
title: Koopman Lifting for Linear Encrypted Control of Nonlinear Systems: Applications to LQR and MPC

summary: Metal halide perovskites have spin-orbit coupling among the strongest in semiconductors, yet whether their centrosymmetric bulk phases can convert charge current into spin current, and what controls the response, is unknown. Here we identify, from first-principles calculations on the four all-inorganic compounds CsBX3 (B = Pb, Sn; X = Br, I), the factors that govern their intrinsic spin Hall conductivity. The conductivity arises from the spin Berry curvature of the spin-orbit-split halide-p bands, 1.1-2.6 eV below the valence band maximum, and exceeds that of III-V and group-IV semiconductors when the Fermi level lies inside them. Because the valence band maximum is an s-p singlet, shifted only in second order, these contributions cancel in the undoped compounds, which respond like conventional semiconductors. With hole doping the response recovers, and at densities reachable by electric double-layer gating CsPbI3 attains the spin Hall conductivity of p-GaAs. The response is therefore determined by the position of the halide-p bands relative to the valence band maximum, not by the atomic spin-orbit constant, a criterion that applies to any semiconductor with an orbital-singlet band edge. These results point to CsPbI3 as a candidate gate-controlled source of spin current for perovskite spin-orbit torque devices.
title: Origin and hole-density dependence of the intrinsic spin Hall conductivity in inorganic halide perovskites

summary: Tuning existing vehicle controllers for motion-sickness reduction requires a desired vehicle response that reflects physiological comfort. The six-degree-of-freedom subjective vertical conflict (6DoF-SVC) model can evaluate sensory conflict induced by vehicle motion, but it does not directly provide a target motion for controller design. This paper proposes a 2-step framework to construct such a reference. First, a target SVC trajectory is generated from the baseline response by limiting conflict peaks while imposing a minimum activity level. Second, a lifted linear model identified using Deep KoopmanU with Control (DKUC) is inverted to map the target SVC trajectory to a regularized reference expressed in vehicle-acceleration and angular-velocity coordinates. The resulting motion reference is then used in an Iterative Feedback Tuning (IFT)-style procedure for fixed-structure PI and LQR controllers. In the considered simulation scenario, the selected SVC target reduces the sequence norm by 6.95\% relative to the baseline. Controller tuning with reduced response models decreases the regularized PI and LQR objectives by 49.5\% and 32.3\%, respectively. These results show that a nonlinear physiological comfort objective can be converted into a practical motion reference for tuning fixed-structure vehicle controllers.
title: Motion-Sickness-Aware Vehicle Control via DKUC-Based Inverse Design and Iterative Feedback Tuning

summary: To develop and evaluate an uncertainty-aware multimodal learning framework for predicting radiation-induced xerostomia in patients receiving head-and-neck cancer radiotherapy. We developed a Bidirectional Attention-enhanced Diffusion Transformer (BA-DiT) that combines self-supervised multimodal representation learning with supervised Bayesian fine-tuning. The model integrates pretreatment CT images and three-dimensional dose distributions, focusing on bilateral parotid glands while incorporating surrounding anatomical and dosimetric information. During pretraining, bidirectional cross-attention integrates anatomical and dosimetric features, while a latent Diffusion Transformer learns joint representations through diffusion-based learning, feature reconstruction, and contrastive alignment. Supervised fine-tuning employs a Bayesian classifier to predict individualized xerostomia risk and quantify predictive uncertainty, with a learnable label-transition model accounting for potential toxicity label uncertainty. BA-DiT was developed using four independent cohorts (Moffitt, Emory, MSHS, and TCIA) and evaluated against baseline and ablation models. Evaluation included predictive performance, calibration, uncertainty quantification, decision curve analysis, and patient-level case studies. In independent MSHS and Emory cohorts, BA-DiT achieved AUCs of 0.83 and 0.80, respectively, outperforming baseline models. Predictive uncertainty peaked near the decision boundary, with aleatoric uncertainty being the predominant component. Uncertainty-based selective prediction generally improved net benefit among retained patients, with greater gains at lower prediction coverage. BA-DiT enables individualized xerostomia risk prediction while providing complementary uncertainty estimates, potentially supporting informed clinical decision-making and personalized toxicity management.
title: Uncertainty-Aware Multimodal Deep Learning for Prediction of Radiation-Induced Xerostomia in Head and Neck Cancer

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [REVERSE]
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that translate user requests into sequences of local tool invocations. While prior cache-based side-channel attacks target the locally deployed models, they typically require the adversary to share model-related components or hardware resources with the victim's inference process. These assumptions do not apply to the predominant agentic settings, in which commercial LLMs execute on vendor-controlled infrastructure. We show that agentic execution exposes a more practical attack surface: although inference remains remote, tools are executed on the user's machine and commonly rely on shared system libraries. In this paper, we first systematically evaluate Flush+Reload and Prime+Probe for monitoring agentic tool invocations. Our evaluation across three hardware platforms shows that Flush+Reload enables accurate, real-time tool monitoring, whereas Prime+Probe, despite supporting cross-VM attacks, incurs prohibitive monitoring overhead and suffers from cache-set aliasing. We present ToolPulse, a cache-based side-channel eavesdropping framework against tool-using agents. We first design the Tool Recovery Attack to reconstruct an agent's tool-execution workflow. We evaluate the Tool Recovery Attack on 11 LLMs across Codex and Claude Code. It consistently reconstructs tool workflows, with the lowest F1 score exceeding 93%. We further demonstrate two attack scenarios enabled by the recovered traces. Task Profiling Attack infers user intent across two Terminal-Bench task categories and the Trigger Localization Attack identifies sensitive tool calls in encryption/decryption and model training/inference workloads. Even under substantial system noise on a server shared by approximately 20 users, both Task Profiling Attack and Trigger Localization Attack maintain high accuracy.
title: ToolPulse: Side-Channel Eavesdropping on Tool-Using LLM Agents
