summary: The Default Relative Domination Principle (DRDP) is a proposed human psychological framework concerned with the possibility that an individual may experience an unearned sense of relative self-elevation after observing the decline, failure, or downward movement of another person. The central proposition is that an observer may experience a favorable comparative shift without making a corresponding objective improvement, acquisition, or additional effort. The proposed framework includes familiar and unfamiliar individuals, relationship-independent activation, spontaneous self-other comparison, relative-gap perception, latent ego-related activation, conscious and unconscious processing, and possible affective gratification, relief, stability, and perceived security. The framework preserves a five-stage human mechanism: observed decline, spontaneous comparison, relative-gap perception, ego-related activation, and possible affective gratification. It further distinguishes conscious ego-gratification from unconscious ego-gratification and both from the possible activation of a latent ego-related tendency. DRDP does not assert that every human being experiences pleasure whenever another person declines. Rather, it proposes a potentially recurring human tendency whose activation may depend on comparability, perceived relevance, relationship conditions, empathy, self-evaluation, and other contextual factors. The manuscript distinguishes the proposed construct from social comparison, schadenfreude, downward comparison, self-evaluation maintenance, and related psychological explanations. A formal mathematical architecture is developed to separate objective position, subjective relative position, latent ego-related activation, self-elevation, gratification, and perceived security. Sixteen theoretical layers, multidisciplinary research domains, ten hypotheses, boundary conditions, alternative explanations, operational definitions, and an empirical validation roadmap are specified. No new participant data or experimental findings are reported. The present work is a theoretical formulation whose distinctiveness, reliability, causal structure, and generalizability require independent testing. Keywords: Default Relative Domination Principle; Relative Self-Elevation; Latent Ego Activation; Social Comparison; Schadenfreude; Unconscious Processing; Conscious Ego Gratification; Human Psychology; Self-Evaluation; Affective Psychology.

summary: Abstract This document gives a technical and functional description of Algorithmic Logic Fingerprints (ALF): a way to verify that an AI model or algorithm in production still makes the decisions that were reviewed and approved, and to stop its output from taking effect if it does not. The problem. Current AI trust mechanisms prove identity and origin, not behaviour: Model signing (OpenSSF Model Signing, led by Google, NVIDIA and HiddenLayer; NVIDIA NGC signed models) proves which file a model is. Attestation and transparency logs (for example Apple Private Cloud Compute) prove which software a server runs. Neither shows what the model actually decides. A model can be fine-tuned, quantised, wrapped in a prompt or proxy layer, or replaced behind the same name or signature, and an AI agent can act on its output before anyone notices. How it works. Fingerprint generation. A compact cryptographic fingerprint of decision behaviour is created without access to source code, model weights or training data. For machine-learning models it is built by sampling decision boundaries. For rule-based or traditional code it is built from normalised control-flow and decision structure. Sealed-probe verification. In the highest-assurance mode, the model is tested with a sealed set of inputs that the computing system cannot see in advance. Four views must match together: decision boundaries, monotonicity and consistency, constraint activation, and constraint topology. A different model wrapped to imitate the approved one cannot pass all four. Approved-fingerprint registry. Each approved model or algorithm version has a reference fingerprint that can be checked at any time. Run-time check at the point of effect. Inside a trusted execution environment (for example a confidential VM or a confidential GPU), the live fingerprint is compared with the approved one after computation finishes and before the output is used. Fail-closed enforcement. If the fingerprint does not match, approval is automatically invalidated and the output is withheld. The capability needed to act (send, pay, move, transmit) is not released. Validation receipts. Each decision produces a tamper-evident receipt anchored in a ledger, for audit and incident analysis. Where it applies. The same mechanism applies to AI agents and model-serving platforms, payment and digital-currency systems (including offline wallets), vehicles and robots, and satellites. It complements existing technology rather than replacing it: model signing and model registries (NVIDIA NGC, Google Kaggle); verifiable and confidential AI clouds (Apple Private Cloud Compute, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, AWS, and NVIDIA, Intel and AMD confidential hardware); agent platforms (Google, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services); payment flows (Visa, Mastercard, PayPal, Ant Group); vehicle software governance under UN Regulation 156; Chinese AI platforms (Alibaba, Baidu, ByteDance, Tencent, Huawei, Zhipu AI). It also gives a technical signal for the EU AI Act's substantial-modification rule and for China's generative AI filing regime, both of which depend on knowing whether the deployed system is the one that was assessed. Source disclosure. This architecture is described in International Application PCT/IB2026/053385 (filed 07.04.2026, published 04.06.2026 as WO/2026/115520; https://patentscope.wipo.int/search/en/detail.jsf?docId=WO2026115520 ). That application claims priority from Indian applications 202531130168, 202631007467 and 202631018571. The related application PCT/IB2026/055615 (filed 4 June 2026, publicly disclosed 16 July 2026) claims priority from it. Author: Sangam Das. summary: The Boundary-Coupled Threat-Transduction Framework (BCTTF) is proposed as a cross-domain theoretical architecture for examining how an element initially external to a system can become incorporated into the system's effective or identity-related boundary, and how a threat to that element may subsequently be processed as a threat to the system itself. The framework retains two principal branches: a subjective-agent branch, centred on identity-related defence in human systems, and a mechanical and automated branch, centred on operational dependency and fault response. Its central question concerns why a system may defend a deeply connected external element even when the system has no immediate direct material or physical-survival requirement to protect that element. The framework formalizes a twelve-stage default mechanism, eighteen analytical layers, two primary case studies, branch-specific mathematical models, parameter-estimation procedures, operational definitions, falsifiability conditions, and a computational simulation design. A supplied Python implementation was executed using synthetic data only. Its parameter-recovery and held-out prediction results demonstrate numerical consistency under the script's own data-generating assumptions; they do not establish empirical validity, universality, or originality. The manuscript therefore distinguishes the proposed general mechanism from branch-specific implementations and distinguishes synthetic model verification from empirical validation. boundary incorporation; threat transduction; identity-related defence; operational coupling; homeostasis; fault response; parameter estimation; system dynamics; computational simulation; cross-domain modelling

summary: Abstract Introduction: The polymeric product obtained in the presence of microheterogeneous catalytic systems is characterized by a fairly reasonable molecular weight distribution (MWD), resulting from kinetically non-equivalent active centers (ACs) in the system that initiates the polymerization process. The nature and composition of the ACs are determined by defining and solving an inverse problem in MWD formation. This problem is acute because revealing the nature of the kinetic heterogeneity explains the changes in molecular parameters and product consumption for different catalyst compositions and propagation modes in polymerizations. Objective: This study aimed to develop methods and algorithms for interpreting gel chromatograms to analyze the kinetic heterogeneity of an industrially obtained polymeric product in microheterogeneous catalytic systems. Methods: The solution method assumes that the MWD formed is a superposition of distributions inherent to each type of AC. Since the problem in the final formulation refers to Fredholm integral equations of the first type, the regularization method of A. N. Tikhonov is used for its numerical solution, with the original problem being preliminarily discretized. This methodology and the developed software algorithms were used to determine the kinetic heterogeneity of catalytic systems containing titanium and neodymium. Results and discussion: MWD analysis revealed two types of CAs with an average molecular weight of A̅T1 - lnM = 11.3 and B̅T1 - lnM = 13.2 in the titanium catalyst, and three types of A̅Nd - lnM = 11.1, B̅Nd - lnM = 12.7 and C̅Nd - lnM = 14 for the neodymium catalyst, respectively. Conclusions: Repeated computational experiments under different polymerization conditions and requirements for the preparation of a catalytic system allow us to reveal a relationship with the resulting heterogeneity of CAs. It allows us to define and solve problems related to controlling the molecular characteristics of the resulting polymer product. A natureza e a composição dos ACs são determinadas definindo e resolvendo um problema inverso na formação de MWD. Este problema é agudo porque revelar a natureza da heterogeneidade cinética explica as mudanças nos parâmetros moleculares e de consumo do produto para diferentes composições de catalisador e modos de propagação em polimerizações. summary: Reproducible by Seed? Not on GPUs: Batch-Dependent Non-Determinism in Text-to-Image Models Text-to-image models are often assumed to be reproducible when the prompt and the random seed are fixed. The paper shows that this does not hold on GPUs. The same prompt and seed can produce a different image when the request is processed inside a batch instead of alone (batch size 1), and the result also changes across GPU models. Replaying exactly the same call is bit-exact, so the differences come from the execution setting (batch shape, numerical precision, GPU) and not from random sampling. This record provides every image used in the image-level analysis of the paper: 3,536 PNG images from 5 models (Qwen-Image-2.1, FLUX 3 Klein, HiDream-O1, Emu3.5 and Janus-Pro-7B), organized into 10 runs. For each prompt: solo images (batch 1, generated twice), batched images and verbatim replays. A static web viewer that shows these images side by side. For each image it tells you whether it is bit-identical to the batch-1 reference and, if not, gives its pixel MAE. Contents t2i_viewer.zip (~73 MB): the viewer, with a small sample (prompts 0, 4 and 8 of every run, 224 images). dataset_test.zip (~1 GB): the full dataset: all 3,536 images, run metadata ( run.json per run), the viewer data file ( manifest.js ) and the original provenance records ( _source/ ). How to view the images No installation is needed, only a web browser. Unzip t2i_viewer.zip and open t2i_viewer/index.html . It shows the sample. To see all the images, unzip dataset_test.zip , copy the resulting dataset_test folder inside t2i_viewer/ (replacing the sample) and reload index.html . The viewer lets you choose a run (model + GPU), a cross-GPU comparison (Janus-Pro-7B on RTX 6000 Ada vs RTX A6000) and, for Janus-Pro-7B, the decoding mode. The amplified difference map in the comparison view needs the folder to be served over HTTP (e.g. python3 -m http.server 8000 inside t2i_viewer/ ). Runs Ten runs, all in bf16: Qwen-Image-2.1 (RTX 6000 Ada, 10 and 100 prompts), FLUX 3 Klein (RTX 6000 Ada, 10 and 100 prompts), HiDream-O1 (RTX 6000 Ada, 100 prompts), Emu3.5 (H100 NVL, 10 prompts) and Janus-Pro-7B (RTX 6000 Ada and RTX A6000, 10 and 100 prompts each). Prompt ids are shared across models. File names (arms) A0.png : solo generation, batch size 1 (the reference). A1.png : solo rerun with the same configuration (bit-identical to A0 in all runs). B_<tag>.png : the same prompt and seed generated inside a batch (e.g. b16-r00-s11 = batch size 16, round 0, slot 11). R_<tag>.png , C_<tag>.png : verbatim replay of a batched call (bit-identical to its batched image in all runs). Janus-Pro-7B file names have a decoding-mode prefix ( sampled- or greedy- ), each with its own A0 reference. Metrics Computed on decoded RGB pixels. Exact means bit-identical RGB data. MAE is the mean absolute pixel difference (0–255 scale) against the A0 of the same prompt and decoding mode. The values are stored in manifest.js and reproduce the paper. Provenance The images were collected from the experiment servers into two dumps ( T2I_v12_images_full_janus_20261121 and T2I_v12_images_full_nonjanus_20261121_b ) and renamed into this layout without modifying their content. The original manifests (with SHA-256 for every image; all 3,536 images match), the collection journal and contact sheets are kept in dataset_test/_source/ . The SDXL images and the fp8/int8 variants discussed in the paper are not included. The images were generated with third-party models; the terms of use of each model may also apply to its outputs.
title: Batch-Dependent Non-Determinism in Text-to-Image Models: Images and Viewer

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: NovaFabric is self-hosted, open-source replay and evidence infrastructure for AI agents and agentic systems. It captures agent executions as portable, secret-scanned Run Capsules and provides replay, behavioral and structural diff, lineage, cryptographic provenance, assurance, and audit around those executions. The same capture layer can wrap general commands and runs entirely in the user's own infrastructure, from local environments through Kubernetes to SLURM/HPC, with no accounts and no telemetry. It is built around five primitives — Asset Registry, Run Capsule, Replay, Lineage, and Evidence Bundle — and five explicit replay modes (forensic, mocked, semantic, exact, and the experimental intervention mode). Run Capsules can be sealed with the user’s own key; sealing is opt-in. Evidence bundles verify offline using only sha256sum and an ed25519 verifier, with no NovaFabric installation required. Interoperates with established specifications rather than inventing formats: OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, in-toto/DSSE, RFC 3161 timestamping, W3C PROV, OpenLineage, and CycloneDX.
title: NovaFabric: replayable, verifiable execution evidence for AI agents

summary: Software overview ComunicELA is an assistive communication application developed in a bachelor’s thesis at Universidade da Coruña in collaboration with AGAELA and the NTT DATA Diversity and Technology Chair. It provides customisable communication boards controlled through eye movements and blinks, with speech synthesis for the composed messages. Optional integration with Google Gemini supports sentence conjugation. Package contents This source archive preserves repository commit b0793c853177cfb02eed9520cc2bf8e9dbf98d2a . It includes 275 original repository files: Python source, requirements, interface resources, communication boards, training scripts, model files and results spreadsheets. The thesis PDF is excluded from this software package. Archive provenance and a file manifest are added; the original code and licence notices are preserved. Download and reconstruction The ZIP is distributed as seven numbered byte segments ( .part001 to .part007 ). Download every segment and ComunicELA_README_DOWNLOAD.txt , join the segments in numeric order using the documented commands, then extract the resulting standard ZIP. The reconstructed ZIP has 24,287,190 bytes and MD5 cc87f80dd066083f91df13d3d2d23c6a . Individual segments cannot be extracted separately. Requirements and usage Consult README.md and requirements.txt . The Python entry point is main.py . The README also describes a separately distributed Windows executable and board customisation. The executable is not included in this source archive. Google Gemini features require the user’s own API credentials, configured through the environment; no credentials are included. Access and licence The software is distributed under GNU GPL version 3, as declared in the source repository. Retain the original copyright and licence notices and consult LICENSE . Third-party components remain subject to their respective terms. Academic context and contributions The associated bachelor’s thesis was authored by Pablo Páramo Telle and supervised by José Joaquim de Moura Ramos, Luís María Hervella Nieto and Marcos Ortega Hortas. Student implementation and academic supervision are distinguished here for transparency. Universidade da Coruña thesis record . Preservation and reuse Archiving a specific source version with a persistent identifier, documented dependencies and usage information supports transparent inspection, reproducibility and reuse of the technical result. The deposit documents the software associated with the thesis; it does not establish clinical certification or independently measured adoption. Source and citation Development repository . Please cite this version-specific software deposit and the associated thesis when using the work in research.

summary: A pre-registrable experimental protocol for testing whether the apparent "self" of an LLM agent behaves as a localised, persistent substrate ( ātman ), as a process assembled from the five aggregates with no fixed substrate ( anattā ), or as a surface regularity with no internal organisation (null). It specifies four studies: (1) localisation probes, with targeted, mean and random feature ablation and capability controls; (2) framing invariance of self-descriptions across system personas, languages, registers and role-play framings; (3) aggregate-wise decomposition of activations (rūpa, vedanā, saññā, saṅkhāra, viññāṇa); and (4) impermanence and re-composition across sessions with external memory. It treats self-reports as evidence only when activation-level probes agree with them, and controls for instruction-following, e.g. a model that says "I have no self" after a Buddhist prompt. Provenance. The author wrote this protocol by June 2026 and kept it private in his Notion workspace, attached to the lab page "2026-06-10 – Wadduwage lab summer work plan" under the "citta transformer" project. summary: Software overview SMART-TDAH is an educational web platform for visualising and analysing students’ exercise results and progress. It combines a React frontend, a Node.js/Express backend and a PostgreSQL connection. It provides user management, progress charts and tables, four interface languages (Galician, Spanish, English and Brazilian Portuguese), and optional language-model-assisted queries through Gemini, LLaMA and Mixtral integrations. Package contents This deposit archives commit 388620adbd23d7793e3af7fec98c6e46a3fea5eb of the Chair’s repository. The package contains 58 original source and resource files, including frontend, backend, dependency manifests and lockfiles, README and GNU GPLv3 licence. A provenance note and file manifest are added. No student database, database dump, API keys or environment credential file is included. Requirements and usage The README documents Node.js 18 or later, npm 9 or later and PostgreSQL 14 or later. Install dependencies separately in the backend and frontend directories. Configure PostgreSQL and API credentials through a local backend .env file. Start the backend with node server.js from its directory and the frontend with npm start . The backend package has no npm start script in this archived version. Database provisioning and credentials must be supplied by the deploying institution. Access and licence The source is openly downloadable under GNU GPL version 3. Preserve the original copyright and licence notices and consult LICENSE . Dependencies and external API services retain their respective terms. Academic context and contributions The software was developed by Ángel Álvarez Rey in a service-learning bachelor’s thesis at Universidade da Coruña, supervised by José Joaquim de Moura Ramos, Jorge Novo Buján and Marcos Ortega Hortas, within the NTT DATA Diversity Chair’s solidarity thesis programme. The project involved educational collaboration with Floriano and Barão de Grajaú, Brazil. Institutional thesis record . Preservation and reuse A version-specific source archive with a persistent identifier, dependency information and deployment documentation supports transparent inspection, reproducibility and adaptation by educational and research institutions. The deposit describes a technical and educational result; it does not establish diagnostic validity, clinical certification or independently quantified adoption. Source and citation Chair’s repository ; student’s repository . Please cite this software version and the associated thesis when using the work in research.
title: SMART-TDAH: Open-Source Web Platform for Educational Progress Analysis and AI-Assisted Queries

summary: The analytical modeling of a plasma wakefield driven by a relativistic proton beam is an element in optimizing advanced plasma-based acceleration schemes. In this work, we present a 1D nonlinear fluid framework under the quasi-static approximation to describe the wake potential excited by a positively charged proton driver which attracts background electrons into a density compression rather than expelling them. We extend the classical 1D nonlinear relativistic plasma wakefield paradigm to evaluate the fluid profiles driven by intense relativistic proton trains under the comoving coordinate approximation. Using a two-bunch scheme, our piecewise-event integration model is validated to high numerical accuracy ($\sim 10^{-11}~\mathrm{GV/m}$) against independent phase-space quadrature of cold-fluid solutions, confirming that interface boundary corners represent physical step discontinuities in the second potential derivative. Scaling to an $N=100$ ramped micro-bunch train with fixed $2\pi$ spacing, we resolve macroscopic phase-accumulation and subsequent nonlinear detuning by deriving a piecewise analytical scaling model. This formulation maps the initial unattenuated quadratic coherent growth alongside the flat asymptotic post-train residual wake plateau, which is determined exactly by the conserved vacuum Hamiltonian invariant evaluated at the final bunch-train exit state. Furthermore, the framework estimates the onset of nonlinear phase-slippage that arrests growth and causes the transient wakefield overshoot to decay toward the residual horizon. Providing immediate 1D analytical benchmarks, this computationally inexpensive tool offers a reproducible baseline for verifying 1D fluid and multi-dimensional particle-in-cell (PIC) codes. It also provides a tractable starting point for exploring asymmetric, custom-shaped driver profiles relevant to transformer-ratio optimization. --- This repository contains the UPDATED VERSION of supplementary materials for the preprint manuscript, including: - fig1.py: The Python script used to produce Fig. 1. - requirements.txt and README.md: The package dependencies and step-by-step instructions required to run the code and replicate the results. This work is submitted for publication. Preprint is available at arXive:  http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06458
title: Exact 1D Nonlinear Solutions for Proton-Driven Plasma Wakefields

summary: This record holds the public collections read by the EARC analysis notebook (earc_analysis.ipynb, software record 10.5281/zenodo.23324439), which audits whether a machine learning score depends on units shared between training and test sets. It contains 101 tables from R packages as distributed by Rdatasets, ten molecular benchmark tables from the chemprop v1.7.1 data archive (MoleculeNet), the ApisTox honey bee toxicity data with its splits, three materials tables, the protein GB1 variants of FLIP, the California housing survey and a monthly excerpt of the Mauna Loa carbon dioxide record. Use: unzip earc-data.zip and attach the folder as an input of the notebook, or set the environment variable EARC_DATA to its path. Retinal images and smartphone activity data are not included; the notebook reads them from their own sources. Licences: every file keeps the licence of its source and is redistributed unchanged, except the Mauna Loa file, an excerpt of a U.S. government record. MANIFEST.csv gives the source address, licence, licence text, citation and DOI of each file; the licence texts and copyright notices required by the sources are in LICENSES/ inside earc-data.zip. ApisTox (CC BY-NC 4.0) and SIDER (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) may be used for non-commercial purposes only; SIDER and Lipophilicity (CC BY-SA 3.0) adaptations must keep the same licence. Files produced by the author of this record are released under CC BY 4.0. Citation: cite this record (all versions: 10.5281/zenodo.24443560) and the original source of every collection you use, as listed in CITATIONS.md with their DOIs.

summary: (PT) Este artigo, primeiro de uma trilogia dedicada ao prolongamento do Itinerário Complementar 6 (IC6) e ao futuro da Região Metropolitana de Coimbra (RMC), discute a relação entre a melhoria das acessibilidades e a construção de um projeto de desenvolvimento territorial à escala regional. Partindo da urgência de concluir a ligação rodoviária no eixo Tábua–Oliveira do Hospital–Seia, o texto defende que a concretização da infraestrutura não deve depender da definição prévia de uma estratégia regional, mas que ambas as questões devem ser discutidas no presente. O IC6 permitirá reduzir obstáculos à mobilidade quotidiana, facilitar o acesso a serviços e diminuir custos para famílias e empresas, respondendo a necessidades de territórios onde já existem atividades, relações e oportunidades que importa reforçar. O artigo questiona, contudo, a ideia de que a melhoria das acessibilidades, por si só, assegura o desenvolvimento territorial ou contraria a perda de população. Defende que a consolidação da Região Metropolitana de Coimbra depende da capacidade de transformar a proximidade física em relações de trabalho, formação, cooperação e acesso a serviços, valorizando os diferentes centros urbanos e os lugares que estruturam a região. A reflexão propõe, assim, que a reivindicação do IC6 seja acompanhada por uma discussão mais ampla sobre a urbanidade que se pretende construir, entendendo a região metropolitana não apenas como um território de distâncias mais curtas, mas como um sistema de relações e oportunidades partilhadas. Publicado no Diário As Beiras , em 2 de novembro de 2026, p. 20, na rubrica urbanidadeS . (EN) This article, the first in a trilogy devoted to the extension of the IC6 road and the future of the Coimbra Metropolitan Region (RMC), examines the relationship between improved accessibility and the development of a territorial project at the regional scale. Starting from the urgent need to complete the road connection along the Tábua–Oliveira do Hospital–Seia corridor, the article argues that the construction of this infrastructure should not depend on the prior definition of a regional strategy, but that both issues must be addressed in the present. The IC6 will help reduce obstacles to everyday mobility, improve access to services and lower costs for households and businesses, responding to the needs of territories where activities, relationships and opportunities already exist. The article nevertheless challenges the assumption that improved accessibility alone can ensure territorial development or reverse population decline. It argues that consolidating the Coimbra Metropolitan Region depends on the ability to transform physical proximity into opportunities for employment, education, cooperation and access to services, while strengthening the different urban centres and settlements that structure the region. The discussion therefore proposes that the demand for the IC6 should be accompanied by a broader debate on the kind of urbanity to be developed, understanding the metropolitan region not merely as a territory of shorter distances, but as a system of interconnected places, relationships and shared opportunities. Originally published in Diário As Beiras , 2 November 2026, p. 20, in the urbanidadeS column.
title: IC6: um itinerário para consolidar uma região metropolitana?

summary: Effective Worlds: Objects, Laws, and Changes of Description belongs to the Emergence Calculus series. This free electronic edition is released under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), as a PDF with page numbers matching the print edition and as a reflowable EPUB. What makes a description a useful theory, and what survives when we change it? Six Birds Theory organizes this work around six primitive roles: descent, representability, route mismatch, staging, packaging and audit. Here they help test whether a coarser description still supports a law, compare what different descriptions retain, and check what supports a chosen world. The book opens with a description that cannot predict and a law gained by forgetting, at the cost of a question the description can no longer answer. Readers build states from the questions they must answer, classify descriptions as equivalent, refining, coarsening or incomparable, and separate repairing a description from changing the question. Later units ask what admitted operations require of a state, carry a public theory across representations, choose descriptions that support a joint operation, and show why a readout does not determine a reconstruction. A unit on averaging builds exact ensembles in which evolving and then averaging differs from averaging and then evolving, the structural question physicists call backreaction, without modeling general relativity or cosmology. Readers then construct the best prediction a description allows for a declared target and loss, and carry checked error bounds through changing descriptions. The final unit chooses and defends an effective world for a stated purpose. Scientific conditions, available operations, access assumptions and competing interpretations stay explicit, so each comparison shows what it relies on. For scientists, engineers and philosophers interested in scientific modeling, coarse graining, effective theories, prediction and the philosophy of science. Prose, monochrome figures, worked examples and answered checks carry a complete route; optional mathematics adds precision. The book builds on the introductory Emergence Calculus course; no other specialist volume is required. More about the series: www.emergencecalculus.com
title: Effective Worlds: Objects, Laws, and Changes of Description

The five contracts concern subgroup calibration disparity, identified counterfactual predictions, hard safety-gated multiobjective optimization, intervention-tested explanation fidelity, and independent replication of automated research. Each contract retains a different empirical witness, source population, denominator, strong baseline, uncertainty, named adversary and independent stop. The forty-two reproducible three-dimensional maps are deterministic synthetic numerical hypotheses, not observations of people or deployed devices. No clinical efficacy, human safety or quantum advantage is claimed. Human exposure and use of sensitive data require entirely separate authorization. F146 / Dataset Bias in AI Aroma Response Models at the Limit. Scientific mechanism: observational data provenance, missing-not-at-random response labels, subgroup base rates, time-dependent exposure confounding and groupwise probability calibration. Unit-resolved endpoint: Response model subgroup calibration gap [%]. Strong comparator: nested-tuned logistic regression, stratified constant-risk forecasts and calibrated group-blind baseline on identical participant-disjoint splits. Concealed challenge: sealed site-level demographic-proxy reversal, subgroup prevalence shift and missing-not-at-random response deletion. Independent witness: independent subgroup-stratified blind holdout with verified group denominators and confidence intervals. Stop: unauthorized use of sensitive subgroup information, group with too few observations to support inference, calibration gap exceeding preregistered tolerance or irreparable test-set leakage. F147 / Counterfactual Simulations of Personalized Aroma Exposure at the Limit. Scientific mechanism: potential-outcome identification assumptions, exposure propensity overlap, time-varying confounding, uncertainty intervals and distinction between intervention and passive observation. Unit-resolved endpoint: Counterfactual outcome prediction error [%]. Strong comparator: pre-registered inverse-propensity weighted, doubly robust and transparent parametric counterfactual baselines using matched observations and exposure constraints. Concealed challenge: hidden unmeasured confounder reversal, vanishing propensity overlap and placebo-like outcome shift. Independent witness: independent synthetic ground-truth causal simulator with reserved mechanisms or ethically approved prospective validation later. Stop: violation of positivity, no independent intervention reference, model uncertainty past declared bound or any simulated recommendation that would initiate unapproved exposure. F148 / Multiobjective Optimization of Aroma Perception and Physiological Response at the Limit. Scientific mechanism: Pareto dominance, bounded preference uncertainty, physiological-signal proxy reliability, dose envelope, hard safety constraints and incompatible objective scales. Unit-resolved endpoint: Normalized safety–preference Pareto utility [1]. Strong comparator: safety-first deterministic rules, weighted-sum classical optimization, expert conservative policy and random Pareto-feasible proposals at matched budgets. Concealed challenge: adversarial preference reversal, hidden biomarker artifact and hard-limit conflict where reward improves but authorization is withdrawn. Independent witness: independent feasibility auditor and blinded simulated Pareto-front evaluator including rejected and abstained candidates. Stop: any hard dose, ingredient or human-authorization limit violated; uncertainty hides a clinically relevant adverse response; nonconsented monitoring. F149 / Explainability and Safety Boundaries in Aroma Recommendation at the Limit. Scientific mechanism: local feature intervention consistency, proxy

The five contracts concern subgroup calibration disparity, identified counterfactual predictions, hard safety-gated multiobjective optimization, intervention-tested explanation fidelity, and independent replication of automated research. Each contract retains a different empirical witness, source population, denominator, strong baseline, uncertainty, named adversary and independent stop. The forty-two reproducible three-dimensional maps are deterministic synthetic numerical hypotheses, not observations of people or deployed devices. No clinical efficacy, human safety or quantum advantage is claimed. Human exposure and use of sensitive data require entirely separate authorization. F146 / Dataset Bias in AI Aroma Response Models at the Limit. Scientific mechanism: observational data provenance, missing-not-at-random response labels, subgroup base rates, time-dependent exposure confounding and groupwise probability calibration. Unit-resolved endpoint: Response model subgroup calibration gap [%]. Strong comparator: nested-tuned logistic regression, stratified constant-risk forecasts and calibrated group-blind baseline on identical participant-disjoint splits. Concealed challenge: sealed site-level demographic-proxy reversal, subgroup prevalence shift and missing-not-at-random response deletion. Independent witness: independent subgroup-stratified blind holdout with verified group denominators and confidence intervals. Stop: unauthorized use of sensitive subgroup information, group with too few observations to support inference, calibration gap exceeding preregistered tolerance or irreparable test-set leakage. F147 / Counterfactual Simulations of Personalized Aroma Exposure at the Limit. Scientific mechanism: potential-outcome identification assumptions, exposure propensity overlap, time-varying confounding, uncertainty intervals and distinction between intervention and passive observation. Unit-resolved endpoint: Counterfactual outcome prediction error [%]. Strong comparator: pre-registered inverse-propensity weighted, doubly robust and transparent parametric counterfactual baselines using matched observations and exposure constraints. Concealed challenge: hidden unmeasured confounder reversal, vanishing propensity overlap and placebo-like outcome shift. Independent witness: independent synthetic ground-truth causal simulator with reserved mechanisms or ethically approved prospective validation later. Stop: violation of positivity, no independent intervention reference, model uncertainty past declared bound or any simulated recommendation that would initiate unapproved exposure. F148 / Multiobjective Optimization of Aroma Perception and Physiological Response at the Limit. Scientific mechanism: Pareto dominance, bounded preference uncertainty, physiological-signal proxy reliability, dose envelope, hard safety constraints and incompatible objective scales. Unit-resolved endpoint: Normalized safety–preference Pareto utility [1]. Strong comparator: safety-first deterministic rules, weighted-sum classical optimization, expert conservative policy and random Pareto-feasible proposals at matched budgets. Concealed challenge: adversarial preference reversal, hidden biomarker artifact and hard-limit conflict where reward improves but authorization is withdrawn. Independent witness: independent feasibility auditor and blinded simulated Pareto-front evaluator including rejected and abstained candidates. Stop: any hard dose, ingredient or human-authorization limit violated; uncertainty hides a clinically relevant adverse response; nonconsented monitoring. F149 / Explainability and Safety Boundaries in Aroma Recommendation at the Limit. Scientific mechanism: local feature intervention consistency, proxy

summary: STARLI / WHITE RAINBOW ERA / FAMILY 30 / F146-F150 TRUSTWORTHY PERSONALIZED AROMA AI FIVE FLAGSHIP PROSPECTIVE NONCLINICAL RESEARCH ESSENCE / 2026-11-23 FAMILY SCIENTIFIC DNA / A TRUSTWORTHY MODEL IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY AN AUTHORIZED ACTOR. The five contracts concern subgroup calibration disparity, identified counterfactual predictions, hard safety-gated multiobjective optimization, intervention-tested explanation fidelity, and independent replication of automated research. Each contract retains a different empirical witness, source population, denominator, strong baseline, uncertainty, named adversary and independent stop. The forty-two reproducible three-dimensional maps are deterministic synthetic numerical hypotheses, not observations of people or deployed devices. No clinical efficacy, human safety or quantum advantage is claimed. Human exposure and use of sensitive data require entirely separate authorization. F146 / Dataset Bias in AI Aroma Response Models at the Limit. Scientific mechanism: observational data provenance, missing-not-at-random response labels, subgroup base rates, time-dependent exposure confounding and groupwise probability calibration. Unit-resolved endpoint: Response model subgroup calibration gap [%]. Strong comparator: nested-tuned logistic regression, stratified constant-risk forecasts and calibrated group-blind baseline on identical participant-disjoint splits. Concealed challenge: sealed site-level demographic-proxy reversal, subgroup prevalence shift and missing-not-at-random response deletion. Independent witness: independent subgroup-stratified blind holdout with verified group denominators and confidence intervals. Stop: unauthorized use of sensitive subgroup information, group with too few observations to support inference, calibration gap exceeding preregistered tolerance or irreparable test-set leakage. F147 / Counterfactual Simulations of Personalized Aroma Exposure at the Limit. Scientific mechanism: potential-outcome identification assumptions, exposure propensity overlap, time-varying confounding, uncertainty intervals and distinction between intervention and passive observation. Unit-resolved endpoint: Counterfactual outcome prediction error [%]. Strong comparator: pre-registered inverse-propensity weighted, doubly robust and transparent parametric counterfactual baselines using matched observations and exposure constraints. Concealed challenge: hidden unmeasured confounder reversal, vanishing propensity overlap and placebo-like outcome shift. Independent witness: independent synthetic ground-truth causal simulator with reserved mechanisms or ethically approved prospective validation later. Stop: violation of positivity, no independent intervention reference, model uncertainty past declared bound or any simulated recommendation that would initiate unapproved exposure. F148 / Multiobjective Optimization of Aroma Perception and Physiological Response at the Limit. Scientific mechanism: Pareto dominance, bounded preference uncertainty, physiological-signal proxy reliability, dose envelope, hard safety constraints and incompatible objective scales. Unit-resolved endpoint: Normalized safety–preference Pareto utility [1]. Strong comparator: safety-first deterministic rules, weighted-sum classical optimization, expert conservative policy and random Pareto-feasible proposals at matched budgets. Concealed challenge: adversarial preference reversal, hidden biomarker artifact and hard-limit conflict where reward improves but authorization is withdrawn. Independent witness: independent feasibility auditor and blinded simulated Pareto-front evaluator including rejected and abstained candidates. Stop: any hard dose, ingredient or human-authorization limit violated; uncertainty hides a clinically relevant adverse response; nonconsented monitoring. F149 / Explainability and Safety Boundaries in Aroma Recommendation at the Limit. Scientific mechanism: local feature intervention consistency, proxy

Reconstructible 3D interpretation: Subgroup imbalance versus response missingness calibration ridge. Refutation: Groups with near-zero denominator render rates unstable. F146 RELATION 2 / Groupwise expected calibration error. Candidate equation: ECE=sum_g (N_g/N)*abs(pbar_g-ybar_g). Units: All fractions dimensionless; ECE dimensionless. Candidate equation: R_miss=P(M=1|Y=1)-P(M=1|Y=0). Units: Probabilities dimensionless; result difference in 1. Reconstructible 3D interpretation: Missing-not-at-random selection cliff. Refutation: Cannot compute from observed data without sensitivity assumptions. F146 RELATION 4 / Subgroup effective sample size. Candidate equation: N_eff=(sum_i w_i)^2/sum_i w_i^2. Units: Weight sums dimensionless; effective size in observations. Reconstructible 3D interpretation: Imbalance and reweighting stability basin. Refutation: Extreme weights lower statistical support. F146 RELATION 5 / Empirical group rate interval. Candidate equation: SE_g=sqrt(p_g*(1-p_g)/N_g). Units: Event probability unitless; standard error dimensionless. F147 RELATION 1 / Absolute counterfactual prediction error. Candidate equation: E_cf=100/N*sum_i abs(yhat_i(a)-yref_i(a)). Refutation: Human counterfactual is never jointly observed. F147 RELATION 2 / Inverse propensity stabilized weight. Candidate equation: w_i=P(A=a)/max(e_i(a),eps). Units: Propensity and probability denominator dimensionless; w dimensionless. Reconstructible 3D interpretation: Overlap-limited weight amplification cliff. Refutation: Violating positivity makes estimator untrustworthy. F147 RELATION 3 / Average causal contrast candidate. Candidate equation: ATE=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]. Units: Both potential outcomes in same predefined response unit; ATE same unit. Reconstructible 3D interpretation: Hidden confounder response reversal saddle. Refutation: No identification absent exchangeability and consistency. F147 RELATION 4 / Doubly robust estimating relation. Candidate equation: mu_hat=N^-1*sum[m(X)+(I(A=a)/e(X))*(Y-m(X))]. Units: m and Y share response units; ratio dimensionless; mu_hat response units. Reconstructible 3D interpretation: Propensity misspecification and model failure frontier. summary: STARLI / WHITE RAINBOW ERA / FAMILY 30 / F146-F150 TRUSTWORTHY PERSONALIZED AROMA AI FIVE FLAGSHIP PROSPECTIVE NONCLINICAL RESEARCH ESSENCE / 2026-11-23 FAMILY SCIENTIFIC DNA / A TRUSTWORTHY MODEL IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY AN AUTHORIZED ACTOR. The five contracts concern subgroup calibration disparity, identified counterfactual predictions, hard safety-gated multiobjective optimization, intervention-tested explanation fidelity, and independent replication of automated research. Each contract retains a different empirical witness, source population, denominator, strong baseline, uncertainty, named adversary and independent stop. The forty-two reproducible three-dimensional maps are deterministic synthetic numerical hypotheses, not observations of people or deployed devices. No clinical efficacy, human safety or quantum advantage is claimed. Human exposure and use of sensitive data require entirely separate authorization. F146 / Dataset Bias in AI Aroma Response Models at the Limit. Scientific mechanism: observational data provenance, missing-not-at-random response labels, subgroup base rates, time-dependent exposure confounding and groupwise probability calibration. Unit-resolved endpoint: Response model subgroup calibration gap [%]. Strong comparator: nested-tuned logistic regression, stratified constant-risk forecasts and calibrated group-blind baseline on identical participant-disjoint splits. Concealed challenge: sealed site-level demographic-proxy reversal, subgroup prevalence shift and missing-not-at-random response deletion. Independent witness: independent subgroup-stratified blind holdout with verified group denominators and confidence intervals. Stop: unauthorized use of sensitive subgroup information, group with too few observations to support inference, calibration gap exceeding preregistered tolerance or irreparable test-set leakage. F147 / Counterfactual Simulations of Personalized Aroma Exposure at the Limit. Scientific mechanism: potential-outcome identification assumptions, exposure propensity overlap, time-varying confounding, uncertainty intervals and distinction between intervention and passive observation. Unit-resolved endpoint: Counterfactual outcome prediction error [%]. Strong comparator: pre-registered inverse-propensity weighted, doubly robust and transparent parametric counterfactual baselines using matched observations and exposure constraints. Concealed challenge: hidden unmeasured confounder reversal, vanishing propensity overlap and placebo-like outcome shift. Independent witness: independent synthetic ground-truth causal simulator with reserved mechanisms or ethically approved prospective validation later. Stop: violation of positivity, no independent intervention reference, model uncertainty past declared bound or any simulated recommendation that would initiate unapproved exposure. F148 / Multiobjective Optimization of Aroma Perception and Physiological Response at the Limit. Scientific mechanism: Pareto dominance, bounded preference uncertainty, physiological-signal proxy reliability, dose envelope, hard safety constraints and incompatible objective scales. Unit-resolved endpoint: Normalized safety–preference Pareto utility [1]. Strong comparator: safety-first deterministic rules, weighted-sum classical optimization, expert conservative policy and random Pareto-feasible proposals at matched budgets. Concealed challenge: adversarial preference reversal, hidden biomarker artifact and hard-limit conflict where reward improves but authorization is withdrawn. Independent witness: independent feasibility auditor and blinded simulated Pareto-front evaluator including rejected and abstained candidates. Stop: any hard dose, ingredient or human-authorization limit violated; uncertainty hides a clinically relevant adverse response; nonconsented monitoring. F149 / Explainability and Safety Boundaries in Aroma Recommendation at the Limit. Scientific mechanism: local feature intervention consistency, proxy

THIRTY CANDIDATE EQUATIONS / DIMENSIONS / RIVAL EXPLANATIONS F146 RELATION 1 / Maximum subgroup calibration gap. Candidate equation: G=100*max_g abs(mean(p|g)-mean(y|g)). Units: Predicted probability and observed event rate dimensionless; G measured in percentage points. Reconstructible 3D interpretation: Subgroup imbalance versus response missingness calibration ridge. Refutation: Groups with near-zero denominator render rates unstable. F146 RELATION 2 / Groupwise expected calibration error. Candidate equation: ECE=sum_g (N_g/N)*abs(pbar_g-ybar_g). Units: All fractions dimensionless; ECE dimensionless. Reconstructible 3D interpretation: Weighted composition surface and minority masking. Refutation: Population weighting hides rare group failure. F146 RELATION 3 / Missingness conditional risk. Candidate equation: R_miss=P(M=1|Y=1)-P(M=1|Y=0). Units: Probabilities dimensionless; result difference in 1. Reconstructible 3D interpretation: Missing-not-at-random selection cliff. Refutation: Cannot compute from observed data without sensitivity assumptions. F146 RELATION 4 / Subgroup effective sample size. Candidate equation: N_eff=(sum_i w_i)^2/sum_i w_i^2. Units: Weight sums dimensionless; effective size in observations. Reconstructible 3D interpretation: Imbalance and reweighting stability basin. Refutation: Extreme weights lower statistical support. F146 RELATION 5 / Empirical group rate interval. Candidate equation: SE_g=sqrt(p_g*(1-p_g)/N_g). Units: Event probability unitless; standard error dimensionless. Reconstructible 3D interpretation: Small subgroup confidence width spike. Refutation: Normal approximation invalid for small samples. F146 RELATION 6 / External calibration transfer contrast. Candidate equation: DeltaG=G_new_site-G_training_site. Units: Both gaps in percentage points; DeltaG percentage points. Reconstructible 3D interpretation: Site-shift increase in calibration disparity. Refutation: A hidden label ontology change impersonates site effect. F147 RELATION 1 / Absolute counterfactual prediction error. Candidate equation: E_cf=100/N*sum_i abs(yhat_i(a)-yref_i(a)). Units: Predictions and synthetic reference outcomes normalized fractions; E_cf percent. Reconstructible 3D interpretation: Positivity versus confounder error basin. Refutation: Human counterfactual is never jointly observed. F147 RELATION 2 / Inverse propensity stabilized weight. Candidate equation: w_i=P(A=a)/max(e_i(a),eps). Units: Propensity and probability denominator dimensionless; w dimensionless. Reconstructible 3D interpretation: Overlap-limited weight amplification cliff. Refutation: Violating positivity makes estimator untrustworthy. F147 RELATION 3 / Average causal contrast candidate. Candidate equation: ATE=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]. Units: Both potential outcomes in same predefined response unit; ATE same unit. Reconstructible 3D interpretation: Hidden confounder response reversal saddle. Refutation: No identification absent exchangeability and consistency. F147 RELATION 4 / Doubly robust estimating relation. Candidate equation: mu_hat=N^-1*sum[m(X)+(I(A=a)/e(X))*(Y-m(X))]. Units: m and Y share response units; ratio dimensionless; mu_hat response units. Reconstructible 3D interpretation: Propensity misspecification and model failure frontier. Refutation: Both nuisance estimators may be wrong under positivity loss. F147 RELATION 5 / Counterfactual interval coverage. Candidate equation: C=100/N*sum_i I[L_i<=Ycf_i<=U_i]. Units: L,Ycf,U normalized response; C percent. Reconstructible 3D interpretation: Coverage failure under hidden confounding. Refutation: Wider intervals can trivially raise coverage. F147 RELATION 6 / Sensitivity perturbation envelope. Candidate equation: E_max=max_delta E_cf(delta). Units: Unmeasured confounder delta dimensionless; E_max percent. Reconstructible 3D interpretation: Sensitivity ridge across confounder uncertainty. Refutation: Chosen delta range may exclude true bias. F148 RELATION 1 / Safety gated Pareto utility. Candidate equation: U=I_feasible*sum_k w_k*u_k. Units: Weights sum to one; all u normalized 0 to 1; U dimensionless. summary: STARLI / WHITE RAINBOW ERA / FAMILY 29 / F141-F145 AI AROMA FORMULATION AND DIGITAL TWINS RESEARCH ESSENCE / PROSPECTIVE NONCLINICAL FALSIFIABLE REPRODUCIBLE / 2026-11-23 FAMILY SCIENTIFIC DNA This family explores five falsifiable, distinct and non-interchangeable research contracts. F141 tests blind formulation target-property deviation on authenticated botanical batches and honest mixture constraints. F142 tests a digital twin model against person-independent responses but never claims that a simulated individual is a human outcome. F143 separates sensor-origin shortcuts from independent preference classification. F144 tests generated chemical validity and externally screened hazard constraints separately; unknown toxicology is grounds to abstain. F145 ensures a human operator can prohibit and physically stop any diffuser actuation; an apparently beneficial simulated state never creates consent. Thirty equations and forty-two reproducible synthetic surfaces are testable mathematical suggestions, not empirical model evaluations, deployed hardware or verified benefits. Any future exposure, privacy-sensitive observation or human trial requires separate independent review, authorization and safety approval. FLAGSHIP F141 / AI-Based Aroma Formulation Design at the Limit Scientific object chemically authenticated multi-component formulation optimization. Mechanism mixture concentration conservation, compositional simplex geometry, volatility, oxidation chemistry, ingredient identity and blind target-property recovery. Target Formulation blind target-property deviation [%]. Strong null expert formulator plus nested-tuned random forest, Gaussian-process optimization and constrained mixture design under equal assay/sample budgets. Hidden counterworld sealed ingredient supplier swap and unannounced changes in ingredient assay recovery. Independent witness independent blinded GC-MS composition plus orthogonal physical-property measurements on held-out batches. Rival training batch leakage, selectively easy formulations, hidden fragrance co-solvent, nonconserved ingredient mass and analytical recovery bias. Binding stop unknown ingredient identity, unsafe or unapproved concentration suggestion, leakage of blind reference or failed mass balance. Mechanism state-space digital twin updates, observation drift, subject-independent validation, latent preference heterogeneity, uncertainty calibration and off-policy model failure. Mechanism missing-modality robustness, multimodal signal timestamps, preference-label ontology, sensor confounding, calibration shift and cross-person transfer. Target Preference classification macro-F1 [%]. Strong null frozen preference prior and nested-tuned logistic regression or gradient-boosted models using the same modalities and group splits. F141 FORMULA 3 / Constrained recipe loss. Equation: J=sum_k alpha_k*abs(yhat_k-y_k)/s_k. Physical dimensional audit: Each scale s_k same units as corresponding property; weights dimensionless; J dimensionless. 3D interpretation: Pareto ridge between conflicting formulation targets. Rival: Hidden preference weighting biases ranking.. F141 FORMULA 4 / Batch-conditional prediction error. Equation: MAE_b=(1/N_b)*sum_i abs(yhat_i-yref_i). Physical dimensional audit: Prediction error same property units; N_b count. 3D interpretation: Batch-shift generalization valley. Rival: Supplier identity memorization impersonates chemistry.. F141 FORMULA 5 / Analytical recovery correction. Equation: c_true=c_assay/r. Physical dimensional audit: Recovery r is fraction 0<r<=1; both c in mg/kg. 3D interpretation: Recovery uncertainty amplification surface. Rival: Matrix enhancement breaks simple correction.. summary: STARLI / WHITE RAINBOW ERA / FAMILY 28 / F136-F140 HYBRID QUANTUM-CLASSICAL AROMA COMPUTING RESEARCH ESSENCE / PROSPECTIVE NONCLINICAL FALSIFIABLE REPRODUCIBLE / 2026-11-23 FAMILY SCIENTIFIC DNA This family investigates hybrid quantum/classical algorithms without assuming superiority. F136 separates true conformer search quality and incomplete reference minima. F137 demands a consistent VQE Hamiltonian, active space, electron spin and shot budget before calculating errors. F138 requires blind externally authenticated aroma spectra, instrument holdouts, honest class imbalance and a capable classical kernel classifier. F139 converts quantum and conventional computational overhead into a declared equivalent core-hour ledger. F140 treats advantage as a paired end-to-end time difference only after both algorithms reach an equal target error and their unselected failed runs are counted. The five main endpoints have different units and do not combine into one score. Forty-two deliberately synthetic 25-by-25 surfaces propose experimental questions rather than actual device runs. A classical success must remain visible; no human aromatherapy or experimental quantum advantage is claimed. FLAGSHIP F136 / Hybrid Quantum–Classical Conformational Searches for Aroma Molecules at the Limit Physical object matched-cost conformer exploration of identified terpene rotamers and stereoisomers. Candidate mechanism rotational energy barriers, low-lying conformer coverage, molecular identity, force-field screening, correlated-energy re-ranking and search-time selection bias. Primary Conformer search minimum energy gap [kJ/mol]. Strong comparator best tuned basin hopping, molecular mechanics, genetic search and classical DFT re-ranking at equal wall time, CPU/GPU budget and accuracy. Concealed challenge concealed torsional barrier swap, withheld stereoisomer and shuffled initial conformer seed. Independent test independent conformer ledger with optimized geometries, vibrational stationarity, energy corrections and blind runtime meters. DeltaE_min=E_search,min-E_ref,min. Dimension assumptions: E values in kJ/mol on the identical stereoisomer and electronic-energy convention; gap in kJ/mol. Three-dimensional meaning: Energy-gap valley across search cost and torsion count. Rival: A wrong reference minimum or hidden initialization can fake optimization.. F136 RELATION 2 / Boltzmann conformer weight. p_i=exp(-DeltaE_i/(R*T))/sum_j exp(-DeltaE_j/(R*T)). Dimension assumptions: DeltaE in J/mol; R=8.314 J/(mol*K); T K; p_i dimensionless. Three-dimensional meaning: Thermal occupation ridge over energy separation and T. Rival: Missing conformers invalidate partition normalization.. F136 RELATION 3 / Distinct conformer coverage. Coverage=100*N_found,verified/N_ref,unique. Dimension assumptions: Both denominators counts of reference conformers, coverage percent. Three-dimensional meaning: Coverage saturation surface with expanding search budget. Rival: Duplicate rotamers may inflate apparent coverage.. F136 RELATION 4 / Finite-difference torsional barrier. DeltaE_barrier=max_phi E(phi)-min_phi E(phi). Dimension assumptions: E(phi) same kJ/mol for fixed molecule and electronic state. Three-dimensional meaning: Barrier crests under torsion and solvent assumptions. Rival: Unrelaxed geometries create artificial barriers.. F136 RELATION 5 / Budget normalized search efficiency. eta=N_verified_low/(core_h). Dimension assumptions: N count of unique low energy stationary conformers, core_h wall-clock core-hours; eta 1/core-h. Three-dimensional meaning: Efficiency plateau across cost and complexity. Rival: Unbilled prescreening invalidates the denominator.. F136 RELATION 6 / Energy winner uncertainty. L=DeltaE_min+z_0.95*u_E. Dimension assumptions: DeltaE and standard uncertainty u_E in kJ/mol; z dimensionless. Three-dimensional meaning: Uncertainty-adjusted ranking inversion ridge. Rival: Correlated energy reference error defeats the bound.. F137 RELATION 1 / VQE absolute reference energy error. MAE=(1/N)*sum_i abs(E_VQE,i-E_ref,i). Dimension assumptions: Both energies kJ/mol with matched Hamiltonian and active space; MAE kJ/mol. Three-dimensional meaning: Noise-sensitive energy valley under shots and gate error. Rival: Basis or active-space changes may mimic improvement.. F137 RELATION 2 / Variational ground-state principle. E(theta)=<psi(theta)|H|psi(theta)>. Dimension assumptions: If Hamiltonian H uses kJ/mol then E kJ/mol; normalized psi; fixed Hermitian H. Three-dimensional meaning: Ansatz parameter valley and expressivity limit. Rival: Noise-mitigated estimates need not satisfy a variational upper bound.. F137 RELATION 3 / Shot standard uncertainty. u_E=sqrt(sum_i h_i^2 Var(P_i)/N_i). Dimension assumptions: Hamiltonian coefficients h_i kJ/mol; Var(P_i) dimensionless; N_i shots; u_E kJ/mol. Three-dimensional meaning: Shot-allocation uncertainty basin. Rival: Correlated Pauli estimates break independent variance assumption.. F137 RELATION 4 / Circuit layer noise survival. p_survive=(1-epsilon_gate)^N_gates. Dimension assumptions: Gate error probability dimensionless, N gates count; survival dimensionless. Three-dimensional meaning: Exponential reliability cliff with depth. Rival: Non-Markovian correlated noise invalidates simplistic decay.. F137 RELATION 5 / Richardson mitigation estimator. E0=sum_k a_k E(lambda_k). Dimension assumptions: a_k dimensionless and sum a_k=1; each E in kJ/mol. Three-dimensional meaning: Mitigation variance-explosion ridge. summary: STARLI · WHITE RAINBOW ERA · FAMILY 27 · F131-F135 GENERATIVE COMPUTATIONAL DESIGN OF AROMA MOLECULES RESEARCH ESSENCE · PROSPECTIVE / NONCLINICAL / FALSIFIABLE / REPRODUCIBLE FAMILY RESEARCH CONTRACT This family studies five complementary but scientifically distinct aspects of computational design for plant-derived odorants. The central claim is not that a machine can create a beneficial scent. It is a prospectively falsifiable proposal that molecular graph candidates, predicted odour descriptors, volatility-constrained Pareto sets, oxidation-stability models and abstract synthesis-route plausibility can be compared fairly against competent classical baselines. Each flagship uses its own denominator, measurement unit, external witness, negative-case ledger and stopping authority. Computational syntax does not establish real molecular identity; a predicted odour attribute does not verify a human perception; a feasible Pareto set is not a safety certificate; a stable simulation is not an aging experiment; and a synthetic route diagram is not a synthesized compound. The response surfaces throughout the 819-page PDF are synthetic 25-by-25 numerical illustrations intended to illuminate hypothetical shape, sensitivity and non-identifiability. They are not model outputs obtained from new molecular-generation runs. Future groups should preregister sample inclusion, chemical identity, strong nulls, risk exclusions and uncertainty before examining results. Classical models should be allowed to win. FLAGSHIP F131 · Generative Design of Candidate Aroma Molecular Structures at the Limit Scientific object: chemical-graph generation under valence, stereochemistry, scaffold holdout and provenance constraints. Physical basis: SMILES parsing, valence and aromaticity sanitization, canonical graph uniqueness, stereoisomer assignment, charge conservation and training scaffold leakage. Primary endpoint: Chemical validity of generated molecules [%]. Comparator: expert-curated terpene analogues, fragment recombination and a tuned classical SMILES generator at the same proposal budget. Strong rival: memorized scaffolds, duplicate canonical graphs, invalid stereochemistry, biased molecular-size filtering or generator reward hacking. Withheld intervention: sealed scaffold-family holdout with stereochemical and charge-state swaps. Independent observation: independent canonicalization and chemistry-rule audit plus blinded scaffold-novelty registry. Binding stop: unknown graph source, invalid atom valence, missing generator denominator, undisclosed training overlap or unreviewed hazardous candidate. This evidence contract does not transfer its interpretation to unrelated flagships or human therapeutic claims. FLAGSHIP F132 · Bias in Predicting Molecular Odour Properties at the Limit Scientific object: blind structure-to-odour attribute prediction with bias diagnostics across molecular families. Physical basis: olfactory descriptor ontology, multi-label rater uncertainty, scaffold domain shift, molecular representation and panel expectation leakage. Primary endpoint: Blind odour attribute correlation [1]. Comparator: scaffold-held-out random forest, descriptor-based regression and a pre-registered principal-odour-map baseline. Strong rival: semantic descriptor leakage, inconsistent rating scales, panel bias, aromatic-family imbalance or post-hoc attribute selection. Withheld intervention: concealed descriptor renaming, scaffold exclusion and panel-rater disagreement stress test. Independent observation: ethically obtained independent blinded attribute-rating archive with chemistry identity, interrater statistics and external family splits. Binding stop: no ethically sourced sensory reference, uncorrected label leakage, insufficient external families or unstable denominator variance. This evidence contract does not transfer its interpretation to unrelated flagships or human therapeutic claims. FLAGSHIP F133 ·

summary: STARLI · WHITE RAINBOW ERA · FAMILY 27 · F131-F135 GENERATIVE COMPUTATIONAL DESIGN OF AROMA MOLECULES RESEARCH ESSENCE · PROSPECTIVE / NONCLINICAL / FALSIFIABLE / REPRODUCIBLE FAMILY RESEARCH CONTRACT This family studies five complementary but scientifically distinct aspects of computational design for plant-derived odorants. The central claim is not that a machine can create a beneficial scent. It is a prospectively falsifiable proposal that molecular graph candidates, predicted odour descriptors, volatility-constrained Pareto sets, oxidation-stability models and abstract synthesis-route plausibility can be compared fairly against competent classical baselines. Each flagship uses its own denominator, measurement unit, external witness, negative-case ledger and stopping authority. Computational syntax does not establish real molecular identity; a predicted odour attribute does not verify a human perception; a feasible Pareto set is not a safety certificate; a stable simulation is not an aging experiment; and a synthetic route diagram is not a synthesized compound. The response surfaces throughout the 819-page PDF are synthetic 25-by-25 numerical illustrations intended to illuminate hypothetical shape, sensitivity and non-identifiability. They are not model outputs obtained from new molecular-generation runs. Future groups should preregister sample inclusion, chemical identity, strong nulls, risk exclusions and uncertainty before examining results. Classical models should be allowed to win. FLAGSHIP F131 · Generative Design of Candidate Aroma Molecular Structures at the Limit Scientific object: chemical-graph generation under valence, stereochemistry, scaffold holdout and provenance constraints. Physical basis: SMILES parsing, valence and aromaticity sanitization, canonical graph uniqueness, stereoisomer assignment, charge conservation and training scaffold leakage. Primary endpoint: Chemical validity of generated molecules [%]. Comparator: expert-curated terpene analogues, fragment recombination and a tuned classical SMILES generator at the same proposal budget. Strong rival: memorized scaffolds, duplicate canonical graphs, invalid stereochemistry, biased molecular-size filtering or generator reward hacking. Withheld intervention: sealed scaffold-family holdout with stereochemical and charge-state swaps. Independent observation: independent canonicalization and chemistry-rule audit plus blinded scaffold-novelty registry. Binding stop: unknown graph source, invalid atom valence, missing generator denominator, undisclosed training overlap or unreviewed hazardous candidate. This evidence contract does not transfer its interpretation to unrelated flagships or human therapeutic claims. FLAGSHIP F132 · Bias in Predicting Molecular Odour Properties at the Limit Scientific object: blind structure-to-odour attribute prediction with bias diagnostics across molecular families. Physical basis: olfactory descriptor ontology, multi-label rater uncertainty, scaffold domain shift, molecular representation and panel expectation leakage. Primary endpoint: Blind odour attribute correlation [1]. Comparator: scaffold-held-out random forest, descriptor-based regression and a pre-registered principal-odour-map baseline. Strong rival: semantic descriptor leakage, inconsistent rating scales, panel bias, aromatic-family imbalance or post-hoc attribute selection. Withheld intervention: concealed descriptor renaming, scaffold exclusion and panel-rater disagreement stress test. Independent observation: ethically obtained independent blinded attribute-rating archive with chemistry identity, interrater statistics and external family splits. Binding stop: no ethically sourced sensory reference, uncorrected label leakage, insufficient external families or unstable denominator variance. This evidence contract does not transfer its interpretation to unrelated flagships or human therapeutic claims. FLAGSHIP F133 ·

Formula V=100*N_valid/N_generated. Dimensional condition: N counts of all generated chemical graphs; V percent, failed parsing included. Predicted geometric signature: Validity plateau across sampling temperature and novelty share. Rival: A parser-specific sanitization definition may change the counted graph identity.. F131 / RELATION 2: Canonical uniqueness. Formula U=100*N_distinct_valid/N_valid. Dimensional condition: Counts of canonical graphs; percentage, include stereochemical identity policy. Predicted geometric signature: Duplicate basin at low sampling entropy. Rival: Canonicalization mismatch can falsely increase molecular diversity.. F131 / RELATION 3: Novel scaffold share. Formula N=100*N_novel_scaffolds/N_valid. Dimensional condition: Novel scaffold count divided by valid generated count, percent. Predicted geometric signature: Scaffold novelty ridge at constrained validity. Rival: Training corpus incompleteness may imitate novelty.. F131 / RELATION 4: Penalized graph objective. Formula J=log(p_graph)-lambda*P_invalid. Dimensional condition: Log probability and penalty dimensionless, lambda dimensionless. Predicted geometric signature: Feasible manifold under valence penalties. Rival: Reward hacking can improve J while molecular chemistry degrades.. F131 / RELATION 5: Shannon graph diversity. Formula H=-sum_i p_i ln(p_i). Dimensional condition: p_i relative graph frequencies; entropy nats. Predicted geometric signature: Diversity ridge subject to sampling noise. Rival: A high-entropy distribution can be mostly chemically invalid.. F131 / RELATION 6: Held-out validity difference. Formula DeltaV=V_model-V_classical. Dimensional condition: Both V in percent; DeltaV percentage points. Predicted geometric signature: External scaffold frontier can invert an internal advantage. Rival: A strong classic fragment generator may beat the proposed model.. F132 / RELATION 1: Blind attribute correlation. Formula r=cov(yhat,y)/(sd(yhat)*sd(y)). Dimensional condition: Standard deviation and covariance matched scale; r dimensionless from -1 to 1. Predicted geometric signature: Correlation saddle under rater reliability and scaffold shift. Rival: Repeated ratings or leaked descriptors can inflate correlation.. F132 / RELATION 2: Correlation Fisher transform. Formula z=0.5*ln((1+r)/(1-r)). Dimensional condition: r dimensionless -1<r<1; z dimensionless. Predicted geometric signature: Exploding endpoints near perfect correlation. Rival: High z is unstable for small or dependent test sets.. F132 / RELATION 3: Attribute MAE. Formula MAE=(1/N)*sum|yhat_i-y_i|. Dimensional condition: Predictions and ratings in same registered rating-scale units. Predicted geometric signature: Error valley across label calibration. Rival: A changed rater scale can fabricate gains.. F132 / RELATION 4: Hierarchical rater variance. Formula u_total2=u_molecule2+u_rater2+u_lab2. Dimensional condition: All variances in squared descriptor rating units. Predicted geometric signature: Uncertainty floor across cohorts. Rival: Ignoring correlated raters invalidates independence.. F132 / RELATION 5: Rank-based agreement. Formula rho=1-6*sum_i d_i^2/(N*(N^2-1)). Dimensional condition: Spearman rho dimensionless for uncensored tie-free ranks. Predicted geometric signature: Ranking plateau despite poor absolute prediction. Rival: Ties and censoring require rank correction.. F132 / RELATION 6: Group parity difference. Rival: Small groups yield noisy extreme correlations.. F133 / RELATION 1: Pareto nondominated count. Formula N_P=number_of_feasible_nondominated_molecules. Dimensional condition: Count of identity-unique structures; all hard constraints held fixed. Predicted geometric signature: Pareto boundary shaped by volatility and hazard penalties. Rival: Predictor uncertainty can alter dominance order.. F133 / RELATION 2: Antoine vapour relation. Formula log10(P)=A-B/(C+T). Predicted geometric signature: Safety risk valley. Rival: Alert probabilities lacking validation do not equal hazard probability.. F133 / RELATION 6: Robust dominance criterion. Predicted geometric signature: Uncertainty band separates stable from fragile fronts. Rival: Overconfident surrogate prediction biases nondominated count.. Predicted geometric signature: Time-error basin with oxygen and light. Rival: Evaporation can mimic decay-time predictions.. F134 / RELATION 2: Pseudo-first-order oxidation. Dimensional condition: Both masses same units; Y percent, specify chemical product coverage. Predicted geometric signature: Mass-balance deficit ridge. Rival: Unmeasured volatile byproducts break closure.. F134 / RELATION 6: Reaction-pathway sum. Formula k_total=sum_j k_j. Dimensional condition: Each branch rate h^-1 under common kinetics. Predicted geometric signature: Competing branch rate landscape. Rival: A missing branch falsifies inferred single-rate stability.. F135 / RELATION 1: Validated route fraction. Formula S=100*N_route_verified/N_generated. Dimensional condition: Counts include all invalid/unroutable candidates; percent. Predicted geometric signature: Route feasibility cliff with step count. Rival: Automatic retrosynthesis is not confirmed synthesis.. F135 / RELATION 2: Route yield product. Formula Y_route=prod_i y_i. Dimensional condition: Each step yield y_i dimensionless 0..1, route total fraction. Predicted geometric signature: Compounding yield decay frontier. Rival: Step yields from unrelated chemistry cannot be multiplied blindly.. F135 / RELATION 3: Route cumulative cost. Formula C_total=sum_i(C_material_i+C_process_i). Dimensional condition: All costs in same declared currency per candidate batch. Predicted geometric signature: Budget-feasibility plateau. Rival: Disposal and safety costs omitted from reported cost.. F135 / RELATION 4: Precursor availability ratio. Formula A=100*N_available/N_required. Dimensional condition: Counts in stock catalogue; availability percent. Predicted geometric signature: Stockout singular boundary. Rival: A public catalogue listing is not proof of legal local availability.. F135 / RELATION 5: Cycle-free route indicator. Formula DAG=I[retrosynthetic_route_is_acyclic]. Dimensional condition: Binary graph-theoretic condition, dimensionless. Predicted geometric signature: Graph-cycle fault manifold. Rival: Acyclic route still may be chemically impossible.. F135 / RELATION 6: Expert validation agreement. Formula Kappa=(p_o-p_e)/(1-p_e). Dimensional condition: Observed and chance agreement dimensionless; kappa dimensionless. Predicted geometric signature: Expert disagreement saddle. Rival: High consensus does not ensure true practical syntheses..
